PRAIRIE FARM ASSISTANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. My point of order is that the government order referring to the recommendations contained in the report of the Prairie Farm Assistance Administration Commission of Inquiry is a nullity and must be struck oil the order paper.
I say that the only opportunity I have to appeal against the report of the Prairie Farm Assistance Administration Commission of Inquiry is today. Inasmuch as the motion does appear on page 210 of yesterday's Hansard as a government order under the heading "Agriculture", I repeat that this is my only opportunity to appeal because under our statutes there is no appeal against the findings of a statutory commission. No case can be found where a court of appeal has adjudicated upon a report or a recommendation of a commission or whether a commission has exceeded its terms of reference.
The commission in question is not-I repeat "not"-a judicial inquiry. Any reference to it as a judicial inquiry is a misuse of the word "judicial" because there is no legal appeal from its findings. I suggest and maintain that this is an executive or crown court without an appeal. It is the modern counterpart of the ill-famed star chamber or cabal. The Commissioner exceeded his jurisdiction in many respects and ignored clause 13 of the Inquiries Act. I shall read that one clause, Mr. Speaker:
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
No report shall be made against any person until reasonable notice has been given to him of the charge of misconduct alleged against him and he has been allowed full opportunity to be heard in person by counsel.
This was not done in this case. This is only one of the bases for my point of order, Mr. Speaker. The Commissioner did not carry out his terms of reference as laid down by the Inquiries Act in that he carried out his inquiry totally in the Swift Current area and1 did not follow the terms of reference which related to other parts of the country.
This government order, Mr. Speaker, would refer the recommendations of the report of the Prairie Farm Assistance Administration Commission of Inquiry to the Standing Committee on Agriculture and Colonization for such recommendation as it deems advisable. The Commission, under its constituting order in council and terms of reference, was not authorized or empowered to make recommendations.
The powers and authorities granted to a commission by order in council under the Inquiries Act are of two classes, investigative and advisory. An investigative commission inquires into facts, law, or mixed law and fact, and reports its findings to the Governor in Council. An advisory commission aids and advises the Governor in Council in somewhat the same way as the Privy Council aids and advises Her Majesty's Governor General under section 11 of the British North America Act. An advisory commission must, by its nature, be almost always an investigative commission as well. It first investigates and makes findings, and thereafter advises or recommends on the basis of its inquiry.
This distinction between the function of fact finding and the function of opinion gathering is referred to by J. E. Hodgetts in his article on "The Role of Royal Commission in Canadian Government", published in the proceedings of the third annual conference, 1951, of the Institute of Public Administration of Canada, pages 351 to 367. The distinction between the delegation of the power to make a fact finding investigation and the delegation of the power to give an opinion or make a recommendation is clearly illustrated by the United Kingdom House of Commons procedure on select committees. May's fifteenth edition at page 614 states:
Reports of Select Committees Power of committees to report their opinion- By Standing Order No. 75, a select committee of the Commons which has been invested with power to send for persons, papers and records, may report its opinion and observations upon the matters referred to its consideration, even thought it is not expressly directed to do so by the order of reference.

April 13, 1965
Point of Order
The United Kingdom House of Commons Standing Order No. 75 is as follows:
Every select committee having power to send for persons, papers, and records, shall have leave to xeport their opinion and observations upon any -matters referred to their consideration, together with the minutes of the evidence taken before them, to the House, and also to make a special report of any matters which they may think fit to bring to the notice of the House.
This Standing Order clearly indicates the principle that in the absence of such a general term of reference then, unless there is a specific power to recommend contained in the special terms of reference, there is no power to recommend.
The operative words in an order in council constituting an investigative commission are "inquire into". These are words of limitation. The operative words with respect to an advisory commission are "inquire into and consider" or "inquire into and recommend". In any particular case, the words "and report upon" may or may not be added to the operative words. They are imported in any event. The Inquiries Act does not contain a general power to recommend.
In the present order in council No. 19631896, which established the P.F.A.A. Commission of Inquiry, the operative words are "inquire into and report". In the Order in Council which appointed the Commissioner the words are "inquire into". There are no words in either Order in Council to authorize or empower the Commissioner to advise or recommend.
The specific terms of reference confirm the negation of any power to recommend: they delegate the power to investigate and make findings of fact only. They authorize the Commissioner to inquire into and report upon:
fa) the circumstances leading to the dismissal of-
-etc. etc., and:
(b) irregularities alleged to have occurred in the processing of claims for benefits under the provisions of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the payment of such claims, relative to the crop grown in the year 1962 in the province of Saskatchewan.
So much of the Commissioner's report, tabled as Sessional Paper No. 12A, as purport to be recommendations are in excess of the powers and authorities granted him by the Governor in Council. These recommendations are in breach of Order in Council 1963-1896, tabled in the House of Commons and affixed to the report. They are null and void and of no force and effect.
There is no remedy in the courts against these recommendations so improperly made.

They cannot be appealed; the Queen's prerogative writ of certiorari cannot run against the Commission of Inquiry or the Commissioner. There was no remedy in this House either so long as the report was merely tabled as Sessional Paper 12A. When, however, these recommendations are subsequently made the subject matter of an Order of this House and now appear on the Order Paper as government order No. 78, then this House is seized of them and can and must take cognizance of their impropriety. That order, in effect, brings in as Government business for consideration by this House and a standing committee of this House, matters that are a nullity and void ab initio.
This government order should be struck out as disclosing no business for this House to proceed upon; as frivolous, vexatious and scandalous matter, and as an abuse of the privilege of this House.
If Your Honour has any doubt about the validity of my argument I should like to reserve the right to be heard further.

Mr. Speaker, in replying to this question and to comments made in the House on Friday last with respect to the construction of a broadcasting centre for Expo '67, I believe it would be helpful for Members to have a brief outline of the project.
Some 200 broadcasting teams from many countries around the world are expected to cover the 1967 World Exhibition being held in Canada. They will require radio and television facilities to tell the story of Canada and Expo to the world. As the host country it is Canada's responsibility to provide the basic broadcasting facilities. As the national broadcasting agency, the C.B.C. was asked to co-ordinate this project.
The Corporation's studies indicated that Canadian and international broadcasters combined would require a centre containing not less than six radio studios and two television studios, together with the associated equipment. Estimates were made of costs and the time required for building the structure and installing the equipment. Total capital costs are estimated at $9.9 million, with the initial requirement in the present fiscal year of $2.9

subtopic: TORONTO-PROSECUTION OF CHINESE LANDED IMMIGRANT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: TORONTO-PROSECUTION OF CHINESE LANDED IMMIGRANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Spadina asked a question arising out of articles that appeared in the Toronto newspapers about a Chinese named Ngar Mye Lau, also known as Jack Mar, and I promised a full statement early this week. These are the facts. Early last September the Royal Canadian Mounted Police received information and had occasion to investigate the circumstances under which this man, known as Jack Mar, obtained a Canadian passport. He had been in Canada for some nine years prior to that date. As a result of these investigations the facts were laid before the Assistant Crown Attorney for the county of York on September 9, 1964, and he authorized the prosecution of the man in question under section 58 (1) of the Criminal Code for obtaining a passport by giving false information and he instructed that the man be charged on that same day. An information was laid on September 9 and a summons was served on that day.
Inquiries of the Ministry
On the following day, September 10, Jack Mar visited the immigration office in Toronto to say that he wished to make an adjustment statement. He did not say that he had been charged with an offence, and he did not ask for assistance of any kind. The immigration officials assumed he was but one of the many Chinese who were visiting the office to indicate a desire to make adjustment statements. Consequently his name was put on the lengthy list and no priority was given to it.
On September 11, he appeared in court pursuant to the charge and the case was finally heard on October 15. He was convicted of making a false statement resulting in his obtaining a passport, and he was fined $1,000 or four months in jail. An appeal was taken to the Court of Appeal. In the meantime he had paid the fine.
I should like to make it clear to interested members and the public generally that at no time, so far as I can discover, did Jack Mar or his counsel seek any assistance or advice from immigration officials in pleading his case before the courts on the grounds of the so-called Chinese amnesty program. In any event, after his conviction the Parliamentary Secretary to my colleague the Minister of Justice, on December 16 last, in reply to question No. 2,161 which had been placed on the order paper, stated that Ngar Mye Lau "did not qualify for the amnesty because it applied only to illegalities related to illegal entry and did not apply to subsequent illegalities not related thereto".
When this man applied for the passport he had been in Canada for nine years and had had a period of approximately three years in which to adjust his status and to become a resident in good standing. There is no record that he ever attempted to do this. He did not finally express a desire to adjust his status until he had been summoned to appear in the courts. Neither the original amnesty for Chinese who entered Canada illegally prior to July 1, 1960, nor the several extensions thereof granted by successive ministers were ever intended to give immunity to persons who have persisted in breaking the law after they have entered Canada.
May I say, however, that in spite of the conviction arrangements are being made for Jack Mar to adjust his status in Canada because he did come forward at a time while the assurance, that he could do so without facing deportation, still stands.

April 13. 1965

speechtext:

Member has been misquoted. I told the hon. Member that I would look into the matter.

In addition, yesterday I received a communication from the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare including a petition signed by a number of mink ranchers of the Digby and Clare municipalities in Nova Scotia on the same subject.
The incidents referred to apparently occurred during a recent United States air force exercise which involved several supersonic flights. The area of the exercise extended from the centre of the Bay of Fundy to a location in northern Maine, and the only Canadian territory which was overflown was Grand Manan Island. The routes did not pass over Nova Scotia. That exercise has now ended.
Both the R.C.A.F. and the U.S.A.F. are well aware of the approaching mink breeding season, and I can assure the hon. member that every precaution will be taken to minimize any danger to this important industry.

Voodoo aircraft stationed at Bagotville breaking the sound barrier. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at ten o'clock last night I had just started to outline what I conceived to be the threefold and dangerous effects of the so-called Fulton-Favreau formula for constitutional amendment which it is proposed be adopted by this House. First of all I should like to deal with its effects on a possible transfer of new jurisdiction to Parliament from the provincial legislatures. Even if the Parliament of Canada, the governments representing all but one of the provinces and the vast consensus of public opinion across Canada desired to have transferred to Parliament the power to enact a federal labour code setting up minimum standards across Canada, this could not be done if one provincial government refused consent. The same would be true in regard to effective farm marketing legislation national in scope,
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Brewin and in regard to many other transfers of jurisdictions.
To come to the transfer of jurisdiction from the federal to the provincial sphere, if the Federal Government, the government of Quebec and the governments of all other provinces but one agreed to a constitutional amendment which would transfer some aspect of federal jurisdiction to provincial legislatures, or would confer a special position upon, say, the Province of Quebec, this being thought necessary and advisable in order to preserve Confederation, then any one province could veto this proposal. It is not just the Province of Quebec, as Mr. Lesage seems to have thought, which has a veto; every province in Canada has a veto in regard to this formula. [DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
If this present formula were adopted it could prevent the definition within the constitution of Canada of the fundamental and inviolable rights of all Canadians as individuals if one province said no. In other words, if this formula is adopted we can say goodbye to any effective Bill of Rights for Canada. Indeed, if the formula is adopted we will have a Canadian amending formula but we might well have one which we will never be able to use. How ironic it would be if we were to free ourselves from a symbol of colonial bondage of the distant past only to fix upon ourselves and our descendants very real and perpetual constitutional fetters for the future. Only those who accept a static laissez faire view of Canada's government and Canada's future would knowingly accept such a formula. It is not surprising that there are united in opposition not only those who see a dynamic role for the Government of Canada, of which we in this party believe ourselves to be spokesmen, but also those in the Provinces-Quebec, for example-who desire a dynamic role for provincial governments. Both alike recognize the prospect of frustration if the formula is adopted. The program for which this party stands, for example, would be impossible if a rigid formula prevented any adjustment of jurisdiction between the Provinces and the Federal authorities.
Mr. Speaker, let me quote a few authorities on this subject. The late Professor Norman Rogers of Queen's, later Minister of Defence-and in case there are some younger Members who do not know about Professor Norman Rogers, he was a distinguished Liberal statesman-said this of the unanimity rule embodied in the formula, and it is

exactly the same as that in the present formula:
There would be no more effective brake on the development of our national institutions. No adequate means would exist to give effect to the national will. Our constitution would tend to become rigid at a time when changing currents of social and economic thought call for serious reconsideration of the distribution of powers and the limitation of fields of taxation as laid down at Confederation. The purpose of unanimous consent is security through stability. But political societies are not static, but progressive. If their needs and aspirations grow with the times, stability of constitutional arrangements will produce friction instead of security.
If this was true-and I think it was-in the 1930's when Professor Rogers was speaking, how much more true is it in 1965, at the time of our "greatest crisis"? I would now like to refer to a recent pronouncement by a very eminent Canadian who might perhaps disclaim the title of a constitutional expert if he had not just gone out of the chamber. The present Prime Minister is quoted in an interview with Mr. Robertson, printed in Weekend Magazine just a few days ago, as saying this, and I call this to the attention of those of his supporters who are in the House:
A charter or constitution which cannot be adapted to changing conditions is likely to be inadequate for survival. Consequently the constitution is insecure.
True, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister was referring to the UN Charter, not the Constitution of Canada. Apparently he has not yet been adequately advised on the application of his statement to the amending formula which his Government is putting forward. I repeat that the present amending formula, if adopted, would operate to prevent adaptation of our constitution to changing conditions. If the Prime Minister does not choose to accept my statement I refer him back to the statement to the same effect by that eminent scholar and prominent Liberal statesman whom I have just quoted, Professor Norman Rogers. Indeed, I could furnish him with the words of many experts on our Constitution which are precisely to the same effect. If I may adopt the Prime Minister's own language, such a Constitution is likely to be inadequate for survival. Canada's Constitution will be insecure.
I would like to refer to another statement in the White Paper itself which has been put out on this subject. It says:
The problem of framing federal Constitutions and the procedure for amending them, always has been to strike the proper balance between the requirements of stability and of adaptability. Excessive flexibility and excessive inflexibility are equally destructive to the federal structure.
April 13, 1965

I ask the House to note those words "equally destructive". How true. The formula which the White Paper contains strikes no balance between flexibility and inflexibility. By section 2 it transfers to the realm of inflexibility every part of our Constitution that counts, whether fundamental or not. This wholesale acceptance of inflexibility will, if adopted, in the words of the White Paper itself be destructive of our Federal structure. Surely this is not what Canada wants. Surely this is not what this Parliament wants. And as surely, if this Parliament were free to examine this formula carefully and vote on it without the coercion of Party ties, this is now what Parliament would ever accept.
Why, then, it may be asked, have the Federal and Provincial Governments accepted this formula? I cannot do better than give as my answer the words of Professor E. R. Alexander of Ottawa University. Professor Alexander has prepared an article entitled "A Constitutional Strait-Jacket for Canada" for the Canadian Bar Review, which is to be published shortly. I strongly recommend that anyone who wishes to have detailed and scholarly information on this important subject should read this article which I believe will be in the May issue of Canadian Bar Review. Professor Alexander has authorized me to quote the following paragraphs:
On October 14th, 1964 22 men meeting behind closed doors in Ottawa performed a disservice for this country whose repercussions will be felt by generations of yet unborn Canadians. By unanimously agreeing on a domestic amending formula these men took the first step in bringing the Canadian Constitution home. Under this formula the unanimous consent of Parliament and the Legislatures will be required for most significant amendments to our Constitution.
This is the most important constitutional step taken in Canada since Confederation. Canada deserved statesmanship-
These are not my words; they are Professor Alexander's:
-Canada got provincial partisanship. There was political advantage in arriving at a Canadian amending formula; there was political advantage in giving every province a veto over important amendments; there was no political advantage in preserving the integrity of Canada as a nation.
Yes, we will have a Canadian amending formula, but in many important matters we will never be able to use it. Canada will indeed be in a constitutional strait jacket.
Mr. Speaker, if this is a fair assessment, and I think it is, what is the way out? I suggest that the Government should set up a Parliamentary Committee charged with the task not only of examining the amending formula, but also with consideration of what form the new Constitution, "the bold fresh
The Address-Mr. Brewin start", the "much more comprehensive undertaking" referred to by Mr. Fowler and Mr. Faribault, whom I mentioned yesterday, should take. In this connection I should like to quote and adopt as my own the words of R. A. Walker, then the Attorney General of Saskatchewan, at the opening of the Constitutional Conference in October, 1960, when he said:
We also believe that when this constitution is being developed, the people of Canada should be given an opportunity to present opinions and submissions on this matter. In our view the constitution does not belong to the federal and provincial governments of the country. It belongs to the Canadian people. They all have an interest in the form of structure of this fundamental law...I suggest in a matter of this importance we should hear what interested citizens and organizations have to say.
Again in the Review of Saskatchewan's Position, January, 1962, the following:
An opportunity should be given to all interested organizations, associations, constitutional experts and private citizens to participate in the formulation of an amending procedure to our constitution.
A Parliamentary Committee could be a focus for a stimulating, exciting Canadian discussion out of which a true Canadian unity might emerge and the strong, vital and respected Constitution which, to quote Mr. Fowler and Mr. Faribault again, "is essential if we are to have a strong nation".
There is, as is well known, some delay being experienced in at least two key Provinces in dealing with the formula, Quebec and Saskatchewan. How long this delay is likely to last, I do not know; but the Prime Minister the other day in answer to a question I put to him-and I think it was repeated in reply to a question put by my leader yesterday- said the Government had no intention of indicating what was to be the procedure in the House with regard to this amending formula until after the Provinces had completed dealing with the matter.
If Parliament is eventually to be invited to deal with this formula, why should it not examine it in committee now? I suggest there is no time for delay. We have not got that much time left. Let us, in Parliament, get on with this task. As my leader said, it seems an absurd anomaly that the one group of people not invited to study the matters pertaining to the crisis of Canada-that is what the B and B Commission described it as- are the elected Members in this House of Commons.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this delay in dealing with this matter is not based upon
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Brewin
the fact that the Government hopes that with the assistance of my friend the hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) and some of his followers it can shove this most important constitutional step ever to be taken in Canada since Confederation through this House without the sort of examination that only a committee with power to call qualified witnesses could provide. I call upon the Prime Minister on behalf of this party and I believe with the concurrence of many other Members of this House, to set up such a committee as a necessary preliminary for a constitutional conference which could evolve a new constitution as a basis for Canada to move forward in unity into the second century of her history.
Messrs. Faribault and Fowler in their book, to which I have referred, not only speak of the need for a new constitution but put forward in draft form their ideas of what that constitution might be. They said their book was only for the purpose of provoking informed discussion. I will not be so bold as to emulate Messrs. Faribault and Fowler, but I want to follow their example to a limited extent. I should like to suggest a preamble to a new constitution which I hope is in the spirit in which Canada's new constitution should be approached, and I do so with the thought that many other people will put their hands to this task.
Perhaps I should say that this is my own idea, and I do not in this regard speak for the party which I represent. I put this suggestion forward for consideration and discussion. This would be a preamble to a new constitution replacing what are called the dull and unimaginative words of our present constitution, the British North America Act. Some might think these words are also dull and unimaginative, but I will suggest this preamble:
We the people of Canada, speaking through our elected representatives in the Parliament and Legislatures of the Provinces of Canada.
Hereby assert our determination to continue together as an independent and sovereign nation within the interdependent world community of nations.
We accept and adopt a federal system as best fitted to the needs of Canada.
We believe that such a federal system must be based upon the equal partnership between the two founding races and we acknowledge the valued contribution made in the past and to be made in the future by Canadians of other origins.
We affirm that the continuing compact of Confederation is based upon respect for individual human rights and upon parliamentary democracy.
We acknowledge the special position occupied by the Province of Quebec as the guardian of a distinctive language and culture.

We hereby provide for the distribution of all legislative judicial and executive power within Canada between the federal and provincial authorities, so as to create a strong federal government able to deal with economic and social objectives affecting the whole of Canada and its relations with the rest of the world, and strong provincial governments endowed with the powers and resources required to express fully and adequately local and regional cultural and historic aspirations of the different provinces and regions of Canada.
We further embody herein the means necessary for continuing co-operation between the different levels of government.
We therefore enact and adopt as the fundamental law of Canada amendable only in Canada in the manner hereinafter set out the following constitution:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it is easy to draft preambles, but I shall leave the rest of the constitution for another day, shall I say, or at least until others have made some effort in this regard. Perhaps we shall even have to wait until after a constitutional conference has been held.

April 13, 1965



best efforts. This will require the setting up of a committee and, as has been suggested by Messrs. Faribault and Fowler, among other things, at some stage a constitutional conference will have to be held. If the hon. Member would like to hear my preliminary views on the subject I shall be very glad to discuss them with him. However, I have not more than a minute or two in which to finish my speech, and I shall do so now.
I hope many other Members of the House and many other Canadians will try their hand at expressing what they believe to be the foundation of our existence as a nation. No doubt there are many Canadian poets and philosophers, some of them in this House, who will improve tremendously on the version I have put forward. I suggest that only out of real striving will grow a truly Canadian constitution, repatriated not in name only but springing from the basic thoughts and feelings of the people of Canada. In crop insurance it was the same story. They brought in a program that our farmers need, but it was so crippled by their political fearfulness that no province was ready to buy it. It was left to this Government to
[Mr. Hays.l
straighten it out and make it work. They brought in the ARDA program; then they made such a mess of the whole country's finances that they could not afford to get it off the ground. It was not until this Government took over and straightened out their financial mess that ARDA really got rolling. They expanded farm credit, but again they only went half far enough and left it to this Government to apply the bold approach demanded in this field.
We have to think a little bigger in Canada today than we ever thought before because our problems are a great deal larger. We have to define our problems and then define the goals we want our policies to head for. Our agriculture as a whole is healthier and more productive today than ever before, but we all recognize that thousands of individual farmers still have serious problems. You can sum up these problems in two words: low income. This is the core of the problem we have to deal with in all our agricultural policies.
Since I have been Minister of Agriculture I have studied personally at first hand the agricultural policies in 10 countries. From what I have learned it is my considered opinion that Canada today is behind most of those countries in establishing policies that will ensure a strong, economically sound food production industry for the expanded population we will have in the future. Where we are most behind is in establishing a comprehensive national policy to cover the whole of our agricultural economy.
We like to think of Canada as an agricultural exporting country, and we still do export some 30 per cent of our total farm production, which amounts to about a fifth of our total exports. But we have been so careless of agriculture during the last 20 years or so that today we import almost as much food, in terms of value, as we export, including items like pork and beef and cheese which Canada can produce as well as any country in the world. We do not think Canada should become dependant on world markets for such an essential item as food. It is to see that this does not happen that this Government is developing a comprehensive national policy for agriculture.
This is not the appropriate occasion to go into the details, but I can say this: I believe that the direction in which we will be moving with the proposed National Dairy Commission should provide a guide for approaches to income and marketing problems in other areas of agriculture in the future. If these sound like radical approaches, I defend them
April 13, 1965

by pointing out that our problems are also radical. Handouts are certainly no solution, nor are subsidy programs that only encourage unhealthy surpluses.
We have taken an ad hoc approach to our agricultural problems for too long. The Government intends to develop in co-operation with the provinces a national agricultural program based on economic principles which, as far as possible, can be placed beyond the reach of political expediences. This program must ensure a stable supply of food for our consumers at reasonable prices. It must recognize the legitimate interests in our domestic market of our trading partners. But it must also recognize the right of every farmer in the country to an income that is more closely equivalent to what the workers in our towns and cities enjoy.
We now have labour laws guaranteeing minimum wages for our workers. We have tariffs and tax incentives for our businessmen. It is time we started thinking of a minimum income for our farmers. In 1949 the average weekly industrial wage was equivalent to $2,236 per year. In the same year the average realized net income of farmers was almost the same, $2,283. In 1964, however, the average industrial wage had increased to $4,472 while average farm income was only $3,815, a difference of nearly $700.
I believe that the primary objective of all our agricultural programs should be to encourage a national average realized net income for the family farm equivalent to the national average industrial wage. I think that should be our definition of an economic farm unit. It was with this goal in mind that we doubled the farm credit available through the Federal Government. It was with this goal in mind that we established the Farm Machinery Syndicates Act. It was with this goal in mind that we revised the crop insurance program. It was with this goal in mind that we developed a new utility-based prize program for all major farm fairs and exhibitions in this country. It will be with this goal in mind that we will establish a National Dairy Commission.
Reviewing the agricultural situation after taking office, the Government decided that the most urgent step toward strengthening the position of the family farm was to provide better credit facilities. Without adequate credit the family farm could not be expanded to its rightful level of profitability in our economy as a whole. We have now provided the credit facilities to make this possible. Our farm credit legislation has also made it easier
The Address-Mr. Hays for a father to pass on the family farm to his children and for young farmers to get a decent start. Yet our critics complain that this is no help because you cannot borrow yourself out of debt.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
These people just do not understand the uses of credit in farming. They still think of the family farm as a few acres of badly cultivated land, six tired cows, a couple of worn out sows, bookkeeping on the back of an envelope, a shed or two, a tarpaper shack, a mail order catalogue and an outhouse. This is not a family farm but a welfare problem, and we have policies for that, too.
Up to now in Canada it has generally been left to farmers themselves to develop economic units through their own resources. In my examination of agricultural policies in other countries I have been impressed by Government programs for the purchase and redevelopment of poorly used lands. I think the Federal and Provincial Governments in Canada will have to consider very soon a comprehensive national program for Government purchase and redevelopment of such lands into economic family farm units, which can be sold or leased back to private individuals who can then expect to make a decent living on them. We want a flush toilet, not an outhouse farm economy for Canada. The successful family farm today must mean modern, expensive and efficient machinery; good buildings, costly fertilizers, city style bookkeeping and management, with enough cash income to send the children to universities as city families do, and electric lights and indoor plumbing.
Let us take a look at the kind of family farm that could be expected to return a cash income of about $4,500 a year for the farmer's labour and investment. For a wheat farm on medium land in Saskatchewan he would need about 700 acres, plus the machinery to work it, or an investment of $40,000 at the very least and probably closer to $50,000 or $60,000. For a dairy farm in Ontario to provide that kind of living, the farmers would probably need at least 200 acres of land and 40 to 50 milk cows, a minimum investment of $60,000 and probably more. To make a cow and calf beef operation pay that much in Quebec or the Maritimes a farmer should have something like 500 acres and at least 100 cows, probably closer to 200, an investment of anywhere from $60,000 to $75,000 and upward.
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Coates
This is the reason we expanded farm credit as much as we did, and we may eventually have to expand it even further. This is why we now intend to take the next step by developing policies that will assure our farmers the kind of markets and incomes that will enable them to pay for this kind of expansion.

gratulations to the Mover and Seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I should like to offer special congratulations to the hon. What a shock this Throne Speech must have been to many Canadians who supported the
April 13. 1965

Liberal Party in 1963, for it is a socialist philosophy dressed up in Madison Avenue language. It is the announcement of an impending marriage between the Liberal Party and the N.D.P. Surely this Throne Speech is little more than apple polishing in the hope the electorate will forget what has transpired in this nation since this Government took office. If this is a smokescreen for scandal, then it is too thin and too obvious and the Canadian public will quickly see through it and judge this Government for what it is, a gigantic flop.

The Prime Minister described my leader as Mr. Clean, and he was so correct. No man in Canada today has been scrutinized with greater care by members of the Fourth Estate. No man has had his character investigated in such minute detail or has had his faults-yes, we all have some- magnified beyond recognition as has the Leader of the Opposition; and no man has a cleaner bill of health when the decision is rendered on his dedication to his country and to the principles of honesty and integrity.

It would be an endorsation of fumbling and bumbling, of colossal ineptitude that has become the hallmark of this regime. Surely no Canadian would vote for the continued tenure 22620-21

Where is the action from the Government on the gravest matter facing Parliament since I have been a Member, and surely one of the gravest in the history of our nation? Instead of action we get excuses on the character of the Prime Minister; he is timid, he is feeble, he is anaemic, he is a nice guy who does not like to hurt his friends. If these are the Prime Minister's friends, who needs enemies? But, Mr. Speaker, they do not tell the real story.
The real story is that the Prime Minister is not capable of taking the action that is demanded, and on this basis an appeal to the public will end his tenure in office-a good thing for Parliament and for Canada. The Liberal Party has caused irreparable damage to Parliament. It has left open sores that are so much in evidence today, and the ointment prescribed in the Throne Speech will not heal the wounds they have inflicted on this revered institution.
Early in the last session of Parliament, indeed soon after the session began, on February 20, 1964, as recorded at page 38 of Hansard I asked the Minister of Justice the following question:
Is the Minister in a position to inform the House on his Department's assessment of the extent of Mafia operations in Canada?
At that time the Minister of Justice took my question as notice. Then on February 26, as recorded at page 258 of Hansard, I again asked the Minister if he was in a position to reply to my question of February 20, and he stated at that time:
-I would prefer to answer that question later, and I also ask for leave to discuss the advisability of answering it.
I did not realize at that time, but I can certainly appreciate today, why the Minister of Justice wanted to consider the advisability of answering a question on the Government's assessment of organized crime in Canada, in view of the fact that I am sure the recent Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister would have been very anxious not to have the Minister of Justice provide us with that kind of information; and that a great many other friends of the Minister, important
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Coates people in the Liberal Party, would not have been at all interested in having Canadians become aware of the degree of infiltration of organized crime within the Government of this nation.
Mr. Speaker, I did not realize the degree but I was concerned, because I was aware of the investigation that was carried out in the Province of Ontario and of the indications of the build-up in organized crime in this nation, most of it moving in from south of the border, taking over our great cities. Now we have found in a most unhelpful way just how far organized crime has gone in this nation and what a great influence it has on this institution and on people who have been elected to this institution.
We are now awaiting the report of the Dorion Inquiry, and that will look after one aspect of the situation. But, Mr. Speaker, are Canadians going to be satisfied that this is the full extent of the infiltration of organized crime into the Government and the operations of the Government of this nation? When we see how easy it was for Mr. Rivard to walk out of a penal institution and disappear completely, to become not only a national joke but an international joke, we get some appreciation of just how far organized crime has entered into the operations of governments in this nation. And surely if we are going to remove the smears that have been placed on this institution by the Liberal Party we as Canadians are entitled to more than the Dorion Inquiry, and we should demand it.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join other hon. Members of this house in congratulating the Mover and the Seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I was very impressed with one idea expressed by the hon. Member for St. John's West, which was that education is now a matter of national concern. In fact he went further than I ever did and said that the standards of education were a matter of national concern, and it is a tribute to his eloquence that so far no one has taken issue with him on that. I recall that the last occasion I broached this subject was on the education bill, and the Leader of the Opposition took me severely to task on the question. Therefore I congratulate the hon. Member for St. John's West on the success he has had, because he shows reform thinking.
In these few moments I should like to deal quite emphatically with the whole concept of
April 13. 1385

reform. The Speech from the Throne finally adopts the idea that we must have reform of our rules and procedures. I am sure you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that back in November, 1962, when I made public my views about the Liberal Party and their zeal for reform, I said in my remarks that the most essential place for reform is in this House. At that time the word "reform" was not quite as acceptable as it is today, and I am happy to see that everyone else in this chamber is now in favour of reforming not only our rules and procedures but the whole concept of parliamentary government.
In the last eight or nine years we Liberals, I think, have learned one thing clearly, and that is that we do not rule by divine right. We occupy the treasury benches only if we pursue reform with zeal. That is our whole purpose of being. Sometimes I am inclined to remind hon. Members and some of the Ministers that the Liberal Party was not born in a soft easy chair at the Rideau Club. Nor was it intended or initiated to protect and solidify its establishment. Most hon. Members know that the whole purpose of the Liberal Party, its whole conception, was to be against establishment. It was a party for the individual, and I think this line of view is very well expressed in the Speech from the Throne.
I intend to deal with one specific issue in this idea of reform, and that is in connection with one problem existing today, namely that of assistance during times of unemployment. Most hon. Members will realize that there are eight or nine avenues which supposedly are means to assist people who become unemployed. If a man is fired from his job he then turns to unemployment insurance. This is a federal matter. There are certain regulations involved and he has to send in his card, get it mailed back and so on. However, if you exhaust your unemployment insurance and you are under the age of 65, then you have to apply for welfare, which is a municipal matter. If you are injured on the job you go to the compensation board, which is a provincial matter. If you are over 65 and out of work you can apply for old age assistance, a provincial matter. If you are under 65 and cannot get a job you go back to your municipality. If you are crippled or blinded then a provincial act comes into application.
All these measures deal with the provision of assistance during times of unemployment. Therefore I suggest to the Government that
The Address-Mr. Otto an insurance plan which is a measure of reform is absolutely needed now. We have all these plans, each with a different system of administration, yet not one of them actually deals with the subject properly.
Consider the question of unemployment insurance. Originally it was devised to provide a means to pay for food, clothing and shelter when a man lost his job. Consider again, Mr. Speaker, whether at the present time the $30 a week provided does any of these things. It scarcely pays for his food. What is to become of his shelter and clothing and all the other expenses necessary when a man is out of work?
Obviously our present measures are not sufficient. Unemployment insurance, I think we will all admit, has been a sort of political football. We included within its ambit fishermen, lumbermen and others, and the provision of strike pay. In other words, at the present time the only people who really get some benefit from the unemployment insurance fund are those who already have protection. For instance, if a man goes on strike and draws strike pay, this additional $30 will help him. If a female employee quits her job to raise a family, this sum again comes in very handy. If a man retires but does not receive a pension it also comes in handy.
However, Mr. Speaker, all these provisions have a reserve, and the unfortunate part about the whole matter is that most Canadians are now convinced that this is a sort of enforced savings plan, and they have no compunction whatever about asking for unemployment insurance whether or not they are really entitled to it. In other words they say to themselves "I have put so much money in and I want to draw so much money out". That is not the purpose of the fund.
[DOT] (1:20 p.m.)
To supplement this I think you would be surprised, Mr. Speaker, at the number of people who use family assistance as some sort of family allowance which people save up for the benefit of their children and their education, but when the time of stress comes they have to dip into that. This is another matter that is a sore point with most people. The situation now is that unemployment insurance, and in fact all these other programs, do not provide the proper assistance, the proper measures. This is where we, as the Liberal Party and a Liberal Government, should get our minds to work to develop a completely new scheme.

April 13, 1965
The Address-Mr. Otto I would suggest the following, in keeping with that idea. We already have an unemployment insurance set-up; we now have the Pension Plan, and we have the old age assistance program. I suggest a comprehensive scheme that will merge all these programs into a truly beneficial pattern. I suggest that this be a contributory plan. I suggest that the benefits be geared to approximately 75 per cent of earnings, very similar to the Compensation Board, because this is a much truer idea of help and assistance. I also suggest that there be a maximum annual income and a maximum fixed to the benefits. I further suggest that the total annual earnings be taken into consideration, so that if a man draws $75 a week but happens to be a seasonal employee and during the course of the year earns more than he is entitled to under this scheme, then of course that would have to be refunded or levelled out. I also suggest one other thing, that all people, whether blind, crippled, old, not yet receiving the pension, who need assistance during the term of their employment should be merged into this one plan.
I have one further suggestion, Mr. Speaker, that may sound a little radical but I do not think it is; that is, that these benefits should be payable when a man wants to quit his job and look for another one. Some will say "Good heavens, this is strictly socialistic". I am looking at it from a business sense point of view. I know from personal experience that if a man doesn't like his work and doesn't feel this is where he belongs, he produces to only 10 per cent of his capacity. We should give them six months to find another job. I have done this; I have said "Go and look for another job and I will pay you until you find one". The result was that I was better off because I found somebody else who liked the job, and he was better off because he found a job he liked, and he and the man I employed produced to 90 per cent of their capacity rather than 10 per cent. This is a problem we must face, and I suggest that this type of new, comprehensive plan would be truly a measure of reform in this field.
I think, Sir, you will recall with me that this may be adopting an idea from private enterprise, because back in 1954, 1953, 1952, just in the general insurance field you had fire insurance, theft insurance, liability insurance, hail insurance, glass insurance and just about every type of insurance, and it was very costly. Then the idea of comprehensive general insurance was introduced. I was surprised to find just recently that I am paying
[Mr. Otto.l
less for insurance now, in 1965, than I was paying in 1954, and getting everything covered. So the administrative saving and the efficiency of this type of comprehensive plan would be very beneficial and is very much needed. We would finally be able to say to the people of Canada that we truly have a measure that gives them factual assistance when they are unemployed.
This would remove a lot of the apprehensions that exist at the present time. Some will say this is an interference with provincial rights, because the Provinces are already concerned in these matters. But if we do have-and we have-an idea of co-operative federalism, I think we can overcome these problems. That, Sir, I suggest would be the true meaning of reform, and I highly recommend that our Government look into this matter and that all Members pay serious attention to a comprehensive plan, which is a very much needed measure at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, my first words are those of congratulation to the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. They are both young men who no doubt have a long future in public life ahead of them.
It is interesting to note that both these Members referred to unemployment; they both said they had unemployment in their ridings and that they were concerned with this. April 13, 1865

During the 1962 and 1963 election compaigns, to listen to Liberal speakers and read their propaganda one would come to the conclusion that they were supermen with the power of magic; that all they would have to do was wave the magic wand and everything would be rosy.
However, it did not take very long for this bubble to break. It has become plain that those sitting on the treasury benches are not supermen; that they are mere mortals and are not infallible. They have also demonstrated that they are indecisive, ineffective, lackadaisical, even lazy, and in some cases are not free from corruption. It has become plain that they have not been able to solve the problems, and in many cases have not even been able to cope with them. This was demonstrated by the mover and seconder, who said that unemployment was a serious factor in their ridings.
Another frightening situation is the skyrocketing cost of living during the past two years. This has created real hardship for those who have low incomes and those who are on fixed incomes, and this includes all retired people on pension.
The Speech from the Throne was certainly wordy. It is possibly one of the longest speeches presented to an opening of Parliament. It includes many left-overs and is full of generalities. One cannot help but be suspicious that it is mere window dressing and that, by the past performance of Liberal Governments, they have no intention of dealing with many of the items mentioned. In the event of an election it is a handy document to have, whereby the Government could say this was their program. This is a typical Liberal attitude.
[DOT] (1:30 p.m.)
Members on this side of the House have dealt with many of the items mentioned in the Throne Speech. I intend to deal briefly with some of them. The hon. Member for Simcoe East dealt with the paragraph relating to the price of drugs. I agree with him that it is not good enough for the Government to re-establish a committee to study this matter. The Government has the power to cut the price of drugs by removing the sales tax. It is most unfair and unjust that there should be a sales tax on drugs. I personally believe that the principle involved here is totally wrong. When a person is ill he has the added expense of obtaining drugs. It is not enough that these people are ill and have these added expenses over and above those
The Address-Mr. Stefanson incurred by a person who is well; the Government penalizes them further by putting a sales tax on drugs. I feel this is wrong, unfair and disgraceful, and I urge the Government to take immediate steps to correct this situation.
The hon. Member for London referred to the Income Tax Act and specific unrealistic exemptions. This matter was discussed during an amendment proposed yesterday, and the figure of $3,000 as exemption for a married individual was suggested as being realistic. Under today's conditions I believe also that that would be more realistic, and I urge the Minister of Finance to give some consideration to an increase in income tax exemptions in his budget which he intends to bring down on April 26.
The Minister of Finance and the Government have turned deaf ears to the requests by Conservative Members for the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and production machinery. Surely by now the Government has learned through experience that this tax has placed a burden on Canadian industry and has hindered growth and development. It is to be hoped that the Government will take quick action to correct this inequity and injustice.
There is something for almost everyone in the Throne Speech, but one group has been left out completely, and that is the small businessman in Canada. In the past the small businessman in Canada has been the backbone of the nation. I am sure almost every Canadian has received assistance at some time from a small businessman. Today with the trend toward supermarkets and shopping centres many small businessmen are experiencing difficulty, but as far as the Government is concerned it is apparently prepared to see the small businessman perish and disappear completely. In this regard this Government is apparently void of ideas, and is content to sit on its fat backside and do nothing. I for one hope it will have a change of heart.
I should now like to refer to that paragraph in the Speech from the Throne which states:
You will be asked to consider measures of special assistance to the family farm in both eastern and western Canada.
I listened to the Minister of Agriculture this afternoon but he did not clarify that paragraph in relation to agriculture. In fact I gained the impression that he was making fun of the family farm. His attitude has led
322	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Stefanson me to believe that these are just flowery words which make nice reading, and they are there only for that purpose. The Minister of Agriculture referred to a national policy for agriculture. This Minister and this Government are noted for going out through the country making statements, grandiose announcements and announcements of policy without action to follow them up. They receive press coverage, are interviewed on television, and by this manner of behaviour are able to deceive the Canadian public.
The Minister of Agriculture spoke about low farm incomes, and that certainly is a true situation. It is interesting, however, to note that since he became Minister there has been a drastic drop in the prices of beef cattle, turkeys, eggs and poultry, and a short time ago in wheat. All this would indicate that he does not have a clue as to how to deal with these matters. When the hon. Minister accused the previous Government of not doing anything he seemed to have forgotten that the former Government introduced ARDA, crop insurance, the Farm Credit Corporation, the Stabilization Act, legislation providing interest free cash advances on farm-stored grain, and also introduced acreage payments. All this Minister has ever done is increase the load placed on farmers. His announcement regarding the increased amount that farmers can borrow drastically increased the value of land and has done nothing whatever to assist the farmers.
Perhaps I should also point out to the Minister that although he brought in an amendment to the Crop Insurance Act last summer to provide for reinsurance, it is my understanding that the Minister has not finalized this with the Provinces, although he has had several months to do so. In that regard I would charge him with being tardy in his duties.
The former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) made a grandiose announcement in the House of Commons on July 17, 1963 about arranging meetings with the Provinces to discuss a national highway policy. This anouncement received a great deal of publicity in the press, on radio and on television. The Minister was interviewed on television and gave the impression that this was a tremendously important policy announcement and that action would be forthcoming. What has been the result? This conference was never convened. Why was it not convened? A cost-sharing arrangement between the Fed-

DEBATES	April 13, 1965
eral and Provincial Governments in respect of major highways would have been acceptable to Provincial Governments, and I suspect that is the reason this conference was not convened. There are indications that this Government is discontinuing the Roads to Resources Program. This was a beneficial and useful program, and it was under this program that many of the roads in central and northern Manitoba were built including the road from Gypsumville to Grand Rapids.
There is an urgent need for the establishment of a national highway policy. To help the growth and development of western Canada it is essential to construct a second east-west route. This second highway should follow a northern route. It could easily pass through the interlake area of Manitoba, cross Lake Manitoba at the Narrows and carry on west to Edmonton and beyond. There is also a need for more highways in northern Manitoba to make this area more accessible so the natural resources can be developed. I urge the new Minister of Public Works to get cracking and establish a national highway policy without further delay.
Another matter for his consideration is the need for a policy covering pleasure boats, which are increasing in large numbers each year in all parts of Canada and will continue to increase. This traffic requires certain services, and it is therefore essential to determine who has the responsibility for providing these services. It has become urgent that policy be adopted in this regard.
Members of this Government have made so-called policy statements with a lot of fanfare and publicity, following which nothing has been done. I suggest this is a pattern which has developed among those sitting on the treasury benches. This type of performance is not good enough. The people in all parts of Canada are entitled to something better.
I should now like to refer briefly to the paragraph in the Throne Speech which refers to human resources. It states:
All the great potentialities of our economy are not, however, being realized. The talents of some of our people are wasted because of poverty, illness, inadequate education and training-
It then states:
My government therefore is developing a program for the full utilization of our human resources and the elimination of poverty among our people.
Those are very nice words, but sound very much as though they have been borrowed from the former Kennedy administration and
April 13, 1965	COMMONS
the present Johnson administration across the line. They indicate quite clearly that this Government has far from solved the problems with which it is faced. I await with interest the legislation which the Government will introduce to deal with these problems. I sincerely hope that these are not just flowery expressions put into the Throne Speech for effect, but that the Government will take concrete action. I hope the Government will come up with some good, effective legislation which will best utilize all human resources. It does seem to me that redevelopment of rural areas and the training of workers fits into the ARDA program.
The ARDA legislation introduced by the former Government is the most forward looking legislation introduced by any Government. Another paragraph of the Throne Speech refers to ARDA as follows:
You will be asked to approve the creation of a fund for rural economic development and, in order to provide for fuller integration of action for rural development, amendments to the legislation regarding ARDA will be placed before you.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)
When the Minister of Agriculture spoke this afternoon he poked fun at what the former Government had done through ARDA.
I think the ARDA legislation was by far the most forward looking and imaginative legislation ever introduced by any Parliament on the North American continent. Certainly it is not the type of legislation that a Minister should treat humorously. As an indication of what the Prime Minister must have thought of the competence of the Minister of Agriculture, let me point out that he did not allow ARDA to remain under the Department of Agriculture, where it actually belongs. He removed it from the Minister and has now placed it under the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve). He has much more confidence in the Minister of Forestry administering this act properly. I certainly will await with interest the amendments which the Government proposes to introduce. The original ARDA legislation had three main aims; to put to better use marginal land that is not very productive in its present use, to develop income and employment opportunities in rural areas, and to develop and conserve the water and soil resources of rural Canada.
On checking over the projects which have been approved in the Province of Manitoba I find that these come mainly under soil and water conservation projects, alternate uses of land and research. Actually very little has been done to date under rural development.
DEBATES	323
The Address-Mr. Stefanson In my opinion this section of the Act is the most challenging, for in the long run it will accomplish the most good. I hope a determined effort will be made to promote projects under this section of the Act. One project which has been approved and which comes under this section is a pilot plant to process rough fish from Lake Winnipeg for mink food to increase the income of local fishermen and make available low cost animal food.
In March of 1963 the Interlake region of Manitoba was declared a test area under the ARDA program, and later it was designated as a rural development area. Many research programs were carried out in this area, some paid for 100 per cent by the Federal Government and some on a cost sharing basis with the province. Some of these programs dealt with research, land use, water conservation, wildlife, tourist facilities and attractions, manpower and the prospects of establishing industry. Many of these surveys have been completed and no doubt they were very useful in that a lot of valuable data has been collected. This information should be made available to area development committees and municipal councils. This information will be of little value if it is locked up. The more widely it is made available the more likely it will be made use of.
In April of 1964 two area resources conferences were held in the Interlake area, one at Arborg and the other at Stonewall. These two conferences provided a lot of information and generated a great deal of local interest. Since these conferences were held, area development committees have been set up throughout the whole district. These committees are doing a lot of good work, and the men and women serving on them and giving of their time and effort deserve a lot of credit. With the spirit of the people at the local level, I am sure that the ARDA program will be made good use of in the Interlake area.
These people, however, need a lot of encouragement from both provincial and federal officials. I am aware that these officials are doing a good job, but I should like to suggest that in an area which has been designated as a rural development area an even greater degree of co-operation and effort should be put forth by officials of both governments.
The Minister of Forestry, who is in charge of administering the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, has, I understand, great confidence in the Act. For this
324	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Stefanson I am very thankful. However, I have one criticism to make. With the original agreement which was signed in 1962 now expired, the Minister has not signed the new agreement with the provinces. In my opinion this is being tardy. I urge the Minister to take care of this without further delay. I also urge the Minister and his officials to do everything in their power to make sure this legislation does what it was set up to do, and that they make all possible assistance available to areas designated as development areas. The success of this legislation will help to make Canada a better place in which to live.
In the paragraph of the Speech from the Throne dealing with ARDA there is reference to the creation of a fund for rural economic development. I certainly hope that when the fund is created the money will be spent all across Canada. My constituency could benefit a great deal if some of the money was used in that particular area, and I urge the Government to see to it that some of the funds are allotted to that area.
There is another matter I want to touch on. I refer to water pollution. In 1958 I had the pleasure of introducing a private Member's resolution in the House dealing with water pollution. Subsequently the former Conservative Government took the first step to deal with water pollution when they made loans available to towns and cities for trunk sewers and sewage disposal plants. In the agreements there was a forgiveness provision to the extent of 25 per cent to encourage towns and cities to undertake this work.
This was the first step to deal with water pollution and it was indeed a most welcome one. Many towns have used this legislation to tackle this problem. But this is not enough. A far greater effort has to be made. The Government of today have ignored this question completely, and by the looks of things they intend to ignore it because I do not believe it is referred to in the Speech from the Throne.
The hon. Member for Simcoe East dealt with water. I would agree with him that water is fast becoming Canada's most important natural resource. A shortage of water is developing all over the North American continent, and it is urgent that steps be taken to conserve water and develop a water policy.
Another matter I raised on one occasion by way of a resolution had to do with establishing a permanent voters' list. In the Speech from the Throne there are these words:
My Government Intends ot make proposals regarding the limitation and payment ot election

DEBATES	April 13, 1965
expenses when it has received and considered the findings of the committee of inquiry.
I hope that at the same time they will also see fit to deal with the matter of establishing a permanent voters' list. Under our system today many people are disfranchised, and there certainly is no reason why every Canadian should not have the chance to vote in a federal election. From my own experience in my own riding I know that if an election occurs at a certain time the fishermen will have gone north to their fishing grounds, and they will lose their votes. I hope this matter will be given serious consideration.
There is another matter which is back on the agenda and is referred to in the Speech from the Throne in these words:
You will be asked to enact legislation to establish an Indian Claims Commission.
We have seen that promise before but nothing has been done about it. I will wait with interest to see whether the same thing will apply again or whether any action will be forthcoming.
There is one other item I want to touch on before I take my seat, and it is referred to in this paragraph in the Speech from the Throne:
In order to raise the level of income of Canadian fishermen, a measure will be placed before you to provide for an expanded national fisheries development program.
I am very pleased to see that the Minister of Fisheries is in his seat. Hon. Members will recall that in January, 1964 the Minister of Fisheries convened a conference which we were all very glad to see convened. Everybody had high hopes that there was going to be tremendous activity and a lot of things done for the fishermen. This heading appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press: "Fishermen To Get New Deal On Aid". Again, there was this heading in the Winnipeg Tribune: "Fishermen To Get Same Federal Aid As Farmers". However, a Mr. Kramer of Saskatchewan indicated he felt that if the fishermen were only going to get the same deal as the farmers they certainly would not be getting much. Nevertheless, fishermen are among our primary producers, and I personally feel it has been the tendency of most countries to forget the primary producer. It is certainly a fact that not much assistance has been provided to the fishing industry.
[DOT] (1:50 p.m.)
This communique, issued following the conference, was lengthy, consisting of 1,850 words. It says here that after the meeting
April 13, 1985

Mr. Smallwood was ecstatic about the conference results. He said there was agreement on all sides to the proposition that the fishing industry should be treated the same as agriculture, and called it a "Magna Carta" for the fishing industry. I would be amazed if Mr. Smallwood was not getting a little bit impatient at the inactivity of the present Government and the lack of action on the recommendations made at this most important conference.
In so far as Manitoba is concerned, Mines and Resources Minister Sterling Lyon has made several recommendations. The first is for an expanded program of biological research, specifically a fish culture and biological station for Grand Rapids, in view of the need to increase output. So far as I know, nothing has been done in this regard. Then he goes on, and I quote:
Much greater effort and technological research, to meet the need for new product development and the development of new fishing gear and technology. A technological research station concerned with new product development was recommended for Winnipeg and an increased program of technological research was requested for both the large lakes and the smaller northern lakes.
I should like to ask the Minister of Fisheries to look into this proposal and at a later date advise me as to what has been done about it. Another proposal is as follows:
Assistance for the University of Manitoba to establish a fisherman education program to fill the need for education and extension work. Additional aid was recommended for technical and vocational training for fishermen in three appropriate communities in the province.
I should like to know also whether any action has been taken on this proposal. The next recommendation was:
Immediate establishment of a Federal-Provincial technical group to examine capital requirements in the industry which requires increased investment.
The last proposal related to the establishment of a fish marketing board. I take it from the results of the conference that this would require legislation by both Provincial and Federal Governments. I should like to know, however, whether any action has been taken on this proposal, and if so at what stage it is.
Before I conclude I should like to refer to one other item which relates to fishing, and that is the shipbuilding subsidy for fishing vessels which is available to fishermen in the Atlantic Provinces. I have no quarrel with this subsidy. I think it is very good; but if these fishermen are entitled to this type of assistance I believe the inland fisher-22620-22
The Address-Mr. Legault men who fish on Lake Winnipeg and Lake Winnipegosis should be given the same consideration. This is a subsidy which is provided for boats of 35 feet or over in length.
I believe it should apply to fishermen in Manitoba and elsewhere in Canada.
There is another matter I should like to mention under the heading of fishing, and that is the sales tax on equipment used by inland fishermen. I am referring to bombardiers, motor vehicles, power ice augers and diesel fuel used for generating electric power. These are items that are essential to the fishing industry, particularly in the area from which I come. An ice auger is used precisely for boring a hole in the ice. The fisherman puts his ice auger on the bombardier and drills a hole in the ice for fishing. It should not be difficult to understand that is its only purpose. I maintain there should be no sales tax on this item.
In conclusion, I hope the Government will give consideration to the suggestions I have made, and not only give consideration to them but will take action to implement some of them.
