speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. members for their encouragement.
The fact that I came here after a by-election held last June shows that the electors of the riding of Nipissing have confidence in this government under the able leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister.
This by-election was held as a result of the death of our friend, Hon. Jack Garland, who was liked by all members of parliament and by all his electors. Everyone could approach him because he was so sympathetic. His decisions were as fair as Solomon's. He was unassuming, but a man of action who always found a favourable and constructive solution to the problems which faced him.
For us in Nipissing Jack Garland had become a living legend. We have lost a close friend and a great Canadian.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with the praise expressed to the movers of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien), who have shown by their speeches that they deserve the confidence of their constituents.
I also congratulate the hon. member for Westmorland (Mrs. Rideout) for the fine way
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Legault in which she made her maiden speech, last Wednesday.

Mr. Speaker, the district of Nipissing, which I have the honour to represent, has a population of approximately 70,000, with close to
38,000	voters, and possesses the whole gamut of requisites for the ideal Garden of Eden sought by everyone. It is composed of 130 townships ranging in size from 36 square miles to 100 square miles, and because of its geographical position could be considered the hub for all future developments in Canada.
It is in this area that you will find a very important factor, the height of land distributing fresh water north to James Bay, east down the Ottawa River and south by the French River toward the Great Lakes. You can appreciate my interest in promoting an extended study of the Grand Canal system prepared by Mr. Tom Kierans of Sudbury, which would affect favourably the development of northern Ontario. It is practically a foregone conclusion that this solution to the serious problem of low water levels on the Great Lakes will come about within a few years. The urgent importance and need for fresh water have reached a proportion unsurpassed by any previous problem undertaken by Governments.
The interim report of the Mines, Forests and Natural Water Resources Committee includes a suggestion that an immediate survey be made of this great Grand Canal system potential. If we put off the solution of this acute problem until later we can only bring hardship to millions of people and serious financial loss to a vast industrial empire. I cannot emphasize strongly enough the importance of immediate action on this project. It would certainly contribute immensely to the development and economic stability of a large territory. You can well forecast the access this would give to great resources and the subsequent addition of secondary industries. This in itself would complete the circuit of water navigation from the Great Lakes to the Ottawa River and to Hudson Bay. It is in North Bay that you will find the centre of distribution for all means of transportation and communication which, as I have mentioned before, will prove to be the main artery to all Canadian points.
Nipissing is very colourful because within its boundaries are found developments for all interests. The northern part, famous for its tourist resource, possesses numerous mineral deposits which have lately aroused the interest
[Mr Legault.]
of many firms because of the large content of iron and copper. We can boast of a granite quarry having a product of quality unsurpassed in North America. The operators of this development have started to produce curling stones, and it is good at this time to mention that they are better than those imported, and that they are the only manufacturers of this kind in North America.
[DOT] (2:00 p.m.)
You will find agricultural and dairy farming in the western and southeastern part of the riding. There are numerous lumber operations and sawmills which play a great part in the economy of the region. We have a manufacturer of explosives in DuPont of Canada Limited; manufacturers of wood by-products in the Abitibi Power and Paper Company Limited, Johns-Manville Company, Weyer-Houser Company Limited. Many sawmills are operated and their products exported to various parts of the world. The potential of the tourist trade will be developed in coming years to an extent undreamed of in the past. The numerous scenic lakes are slowly being discovered by thirsty vacation seekers. The visitors to the eastern end of the riding will find indescribable appreciation of the grandiose, majestic splendours surrounding Mattawa.
Widdifield Township at the moment is undergoing growing pains but is coping with the situation very well with the installation of the Bomarc base and the complex Sage installation which is the nerve centre for the air defence of all North America. You can well understand that because of its position, Nipissing is soon to experience an unheard of expansion.
When I say my riding is colourful it is because of the wonderful and varied ethnic groups of people who live in it and give it an atmosphere of warmth and friendliness never forgotten by all who visit us. It is composed of people of numerous racial origins such as Indians, Anglo-Saxons, French Italians, Germans, Greek, Chinese, Ukrainians, Poles and many others. It would be well to realize that this is a proving ground of bilingualism and biculturalism. In this great district you will find all commodities and services at your disposition. The opportunities are unlimited and the growth is being accomplished step by step in a very intelligent way.
I was very proud and privileged to have been nominated and elected to represent Nipissing in support of the present admin-
April 13, 1965

istration guided by our Prime Minister, a great man at the right time for the right job, who has steered the country during its most difficult years, the man knowing the secret of how to compromise in order to satisfy everyone but, as you have all realized, always achieving a definite goal that had been set. A great quality which he possesses is to delegate responsibilities to well chosen experts in their field. This Government has undertaken constructive measures well balanced to the true economic potentiality of this country and its citizens. This Government has taken positive action to bring about a more unified Canada. There has been a lot of criticism, but we all must accept the fact that the decisions taken were definite, constructive measures for this purpose.
A distinctive flag, a controversial issue for many years, unifies and identifies our great country and its people. The B and B Commission was the only practical movement made in order to study and suggest the proper solution to a problem which faces us, but which was too often brushed aside for fear of facing reality. It is bringing facts to the attention of everyone, which we have to accept and to which concrete, logical solutions will be brought about for a more unified country.
The Pension Plan passed at the last session is a social measure which in itself helps to cement this unity. We have all experienced numerous pieces of legislation which make our country the best democratic place to live in. All this has been under the powerful leadership of our right hon. Prime Minister. Evidence is in the united and complete support and great admiration for him from all members of the Liberal Party, and from many others. This is being accomplished under adverse conditions and the difficulty of fighting off distorted interpretations of various reports detrimental to favourable solutions, coupled with the uneasiness and impractical position of a minority Government. It is the first time in Canadian history that a minority Government has been able to survive for more than a few months and yet accomplish so much.
The Government is sometimes accused of being accident-prone, by innuendo, but certainly not of being a Government of do nothing and be nothing. All Canadians appreciate and support social measures which have as their purpose to give security to needy and elderly people, but we must beware of extremists who would bring about socialism.
327
The Address-Mr. Legault We must leave the citizens of this country free, so that by their incentive, desire for improvement and reward, all shall obtain a better standard of living. The new legislation in the Throne Speech will do much for all the people of Canada.
I would like to bring to your attention the difficult preparation of the comprehensive medicare plan which must bring satisfaction to everyone. We do want to obtain the required protection and attention for needy and elderly people, but still respect the liberty of action, choice and decision of all parties affected by this legislation. The policies and ideals of this Government respecting proper administration call for co-ordination and recognition of the rights of various jurisdictions.
The federal-provincial co-operative way of administering such a vast country is the only logical action to take. It is to be regretted that we as a people have somewhat failed to keep pace mentally with the accelerated technical developments which have taken place. We have to realize such facts as that within the next few years, two hours and fifteen minutes is all that will be required to cross the Atlantic. Immediate transcription is obtained of all activities throughout the world, yet we seem to be immunized against the miseries that exist in most parts of this world. Water always finds a way to adjust to its own level. Racial, economical and social problems throughout this world can within a few hours be our own, whether we like it or not.

Mr. Speaker, the program undertaken for the educational, cultural, social and economic development of our Indians, as set forth during the last session, is one that, within the next 10 years, should bring out the great potential of that capable and very intelligent race.
We often show too much impatience for the solutions of problems concerning bilingualism and biculturalism. The steps taken have already brought about an obvious improvement, but it will take at least two generations before results really satisfactory for all Canadians can be achieved.
I think that the setting up of a company of young Canadians will fulfil two functions. One is the work and the good that those young citizens will do; the other is the education and the practical knowledge that they will get from those experiences.
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Ricard
The revision of the regulations concerning the administration of the Immigration Act will bring about an improvement to the situation that we know today.
A study to reform parliamentary procedure should be welcome by all hon. members. All social measures proposed will certainly, with the years, fill many gaps, simplify and cut the number of welfare pension plans in existence today. That will entail the rationalization of several measures which are now impracticable. It is with such an approach that Canada will improve and continue to be a country that is envied the world over.
A suggestion I should like to make to the house at this time would be to provide money to tourist camp operators as it is done at the present time in the case of farmers through farm credit.

The area development program is very welcome, and will bring encouragement to temporarily depressed areas. This, Mr. Speaker, should prove to be a very aggressive and interesting session.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to pay tribute to the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the hon. member for St. Mauriee-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) for the gracefulness and the efficiency with which they discharged their task in moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
There are many subjects with which I would like to deal, but I will abstain and will merely mention them casually.
One could make a complete speech on the absence of the measures the government should take to stop the ever-increasing rise in the cost of living. At present the cost of living has reached an all-time high in the country, that is 137.3 per cent. In my opinion those who are responsible for this situation are the hon. members now sitting on the treasury benches. It is their responsibility to take the necessary steps so that the income of the average worker, of the factory worker is no longer taxed so heavily because of the excessive cost of living. A moment of thought is enough to notice that the cost of living has risen alarmingly by 2.7 per cent during a single year. This should be enough to urge all the people of good will to do something to correct this situation.

Of course, there is the 11 per cent tax created by our hon. friends opposite which has surely contributed to a great extent to increase the cost of living. The numerous representations which we made to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) urging him to repeal this tax have been unsuccessful so far.
Once again, appealing to his generosity, I ask him to remove this 11 per cent tax which is surely responsible to a great extent for this increase in the cost of living.
I could say a great deal also about the means to check unemployment. We had been promised full employment during the last two election campaigns, and I am sorry to tell the house that my province still has the largest group of unemployed in Canada. I understand that unemployed in the province of Quebec represent 39 per cent of all unemployed in Canada. However, this did not seem to upset too much the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) to whom we have asked, and are asking again, what he intends to do in order to provide some assistance, especially to the unemployed of the province of Quebec and of the Maritime provinces. To each of our questions, he always gave the same answer: You will get a reply to your questions in due course. We have been hearing that for two years and the speech from the throne does not contain any measure that will increase the number of jobs in Canada.
I would also like to point out that thanks to the opposition's pressures and suggestions, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) finally agreed to meet our requests to a limited extent. For more than two years, we have been urging the Liberal government, more particularly the Minister of Agriculture, to set up a price of approximately $3.50 per hundredweight for manufactured milk. Well, some time ago, the Minister of Agriculture announced to the house a dairy policy based on the one his predecessor had set up a few years previously.
However, as he himself acknowledged, he took that decision only after having caused the farmers to lose about $11 million that they would have got if the dairy policy put forward while we were in office had been maintained. No wonder farmers feel insecure. In fact, all of them are peeved with the Minister of Agriculture at present.
Mr. Speaker, my next remarks will concern mainly the Canadian textile industry, and they are made in the best interests of my constituents.
April 13, 1965

Of all our industries, that of textile is one of the oldest ones in this country. Throughout the years, it has provided stable and profitable employment. It is imperative to give that industry, which is one of our basic industries, all the protection it needs. It is found mostly in small and medium sized cities where it enables most of the inhabitants to earn a living.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, if one keeps in mind the fact that last year the synthetic textile industry gave work to about 20,600 workers, one realizes its importance. Those 20,600 workers are integrated into the parish and community life of our cities. They are citizens who pay taxes. We ought to give them the protection to which they are entitled.
In 1964, in the field of synthetic textile, this industry spent about $7.7 million for new buildings, while almost $40 million was spent on machinery. This means that this industry deserves the attention of the government and of the members of this house.
There is a danger that this industry may be seriously affected in the coming months, unless beneficial and drastic measures are taken immediately.
When one remembers that in 1950, the Canadian industry supplied 77 per cent of the local market, while it supplied only 60 per cent in 1963, one realizes that foreign manufacturers are progressively taking over our domestic market, year after year, to the great detriment of the Canadian worker.
In 1964, imports from Japan amounted to $44.7 million, that is 37.9 per cent more than in 1963.
When the Japanese industry started to compete with the Canadian textile industry immediately after the war, its products left a lot to be desired and they were quite inferior in quality to the products made in Canada. But today, conditions have changed and if the Japanese products are not of a superior quality they are at least equal in quality to the products made in Canada.
As a result of the improvement of its machinery, the Japanese textile industry has now exceeded the needs of the Japanese market. In fact, according to the information provided by a Canadian businessman, the Japanese synthetic textile industry is determined to invade at all costs the Canadian market.
According to statistics I have obtained from various sources, we have practically succeeded, up to now, in keeping in check imports from the United States. On the other
The Address-Mr. Ricard hand, imports from Japan increased from 6.1 per cent in 1959 to 22.6 per cent in 1964. And, according to the information I have obtained from that same Canadian industrialist, imports from Japan during the first few months of this year well exceeded those of 1964. There is therefore reason for alarm, and it is the government's responsibility to take whatever action is necessary to restrain such imports which can only be detrimental to our workers.
Last week, I met the president of a synthetic textiles company and as I remarked that his staff appeared to be quite busy, he said: Yes, we are quite busy this year, but unless some action is taken I fear we may not be so busy next year, for if Japanese imports continue to invade our market at this rate, several of our employees will be forced, I am sorry to say, to find employment elsewhere.
Mr. Speaker, the textile industry is, as everybody knows, of prime importance to the riding I represent. The remarks of the president of that company made me think of the employees of Consolidated Textile Limited, operating a very important spinning-mill in my constituency, as well as those of the Yamaska Shirt Company who will also be affected if shirts, blouses, trousers and shorts continue to be imported at the rate they are now.
Last year, for instance, the management of Consolidated Textile Limited spent a great deal of money on machinery improvement, and it would be most unfortunate if, because of this government's inaction, many of my compatriots were obliged, next year, to find some other kind of employment while they have devoted so many years to this particular work.
Mr. Speaker, let us keep in mind that, like Cornwall, St. Hyacinthe has the best employees in the Canadian textile industry.
I have here a brief submitted to the tariff board by the Canadian Textile Institute. A look at the tables it contains will give an idea of the real danger which the Canadian textile industry is facing at the present time.
At this stage I might be allowed to quote a few figures. A table entitled:
Imports of synthetic textiles from Japan (in thousand square yards)
shows that Japanese imports increased from 119 square yards or .3 per cent of the Canadian market in 1954 to 14,853 square yards or 20.2 per cent in 1963. This situation would not be too alarming if our local market could be expanded only up to a certain point.

April 13, 1985
The Address-Mr. Ricard The natural increase in our population can absorb a greater production of synthetic textiles, but our industry already produces a great deal as a result of an improved labour force and modernized machinery.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
What is alarming is that, while imports amounted to .3 per cent in 1954, they are now 20.2 per cent and this is in one area only.
For instance, imports of Japanese rayon spun textiles increased from 17,000 square yards to 85,000,000 square yards in 1963, which means that such imports now supply 15.7 per cent of the Canadian market, as compared to 4.6 per cent in 1959.
Another table shows that in 1959 imports of Japanese textiles (rayon spun goods) totalled 102,000 square yards, while in 1963, Japanese manufacturers exported to Canada
7,565,000	square yards. Therefore, imports increased from 1.9 per cent in 1959 to 10.6 per cent in 1963.
Mr. Speaker, to prove beyond the shadow of a doubt that the Japanese industry, especially in the field of synthetic textiles, is constantly invading our home market, I feel it is my duty to raise my voice and remind the government of its obligations. I am not against Canada trading with other countries, far from it. To a certain extent, we have to depend on foreign markets for our own products, but it seems to me we would behave like an ostrich if we were to bury our heads in the sand to avoid seeing the danger that is threatening our workers at the present time.
It is all very well, as I said, to have trade relations with foreign countries, but our first obligation is to our fellow Canadians. It was in order to remind the Minister of this thing that I decided today to speak for a few minutes on this subject.
My hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Forest) recognized last week the importance of this textile industry for his constituency. I associate myself with him and with my hon. friend from Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Mar-coux), in requesting the government to give immediate attention to this problem. Let us not wait until it is too late; let us take right now the necessary steps.
During a discussion with the president of one of the most important textile manufacturing companies in the province, I realized there is presently great apprehension and people stand in fear of the future in the event

steps are not taken immediately to correct this situation.
I trust that other members, representing
constituencies where there are textile industries, will support my representations and will ask that voluntary quotas be applied on all imports from Japan.
I reviewed some articles which appeared in the Japanese press, and I found out that for the year 1964 only, compared with 1963, Japanese production of nylon goods increased 48.8 per cent, of polyester goods 37.5 per cent, and of acrylic textile goods, 71.1 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, if we consider, as I was saying a few minutes ago, that the production of the Japanese industry now exceeds the needs of the Japanese market and that they are determined to drop goods on the Canadian market, we must conclude that we have to protect ourselves against this danger.
I wish to say that I endorse the proposal made by CATMA in its brief to the department a few weeks ago. To that end, Japanese exports should be subject to quotas of not more than two million square yards for synthetic fabric, four million square yards for rayon thread and not more than six million square yards for rayon fabric.
Unless we take the necessary steps to establish such quotas, our textile industry and especially that of synthetic textiles, will end up in the doldrums and possibly vanish before too many years.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I call upon hon. members to co-operate so that Canadian workers will not have to suffer from the encouragement given imports of products manufactured by others than Canadian taxpayers.

I refer to those measures which suggest that further steps are to be taken in the field of social welfare and that there is to be launched a war on poverty. We heartily welcome these words, and we earnestly hope that during the course

of this session they will be translated into actual statutes. It is our fear that in many instances only words have been given to us, but we shall press for action.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
It is my notion from studying the Speech from the Throne that perhaps the item that is closest to being ready to present to us is what is referred to as the Canada Assistance Plan. We do not have much detail about this piece of legislation yet, but I gather it is to be a form of legislation that will in time take the place of the Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons Act, the Disabled Persons Act and unemployment assistance, and that it will provide certain other benefits as well. speechtext:
We suggest that when the Government is raiding our cupboard it take that one and put it on the statute books, and that it make the full pension available at age 65 right away.
We also feel, despite the explanations given by the Prime Minister, that the Government is still moving too slowly with respect to medicare. We want to see not just federal-provincial conferences, not just talk; we want to see action in this important field. When there is talk about a war on poverty, let it be
DEBATES	331
The Address-Mr. Knowles remembered we will not be rid of poverty until we are rid of all the slums in this country, until our people are well housed whether they live in the cities or in the rural areas. We will not be free of poverty until even in a country where education is a provincial matter we have found a way to make our nation's resources available so that for all our people education can be brought to a much higher level than is the case at the present time.
There is one other immediate item in our New Democratic Party cupboard which we wish the Government would take and put on the statute books. I refer to the need to provide for the maintenance of income when the breadwinner is off work because of illness. This is one of the most serious gaps in our social legislation. We moved a bit in that direction a few years ago when we provided that if a person has collected one benefit under unemployment insurance and then becomes ill he may continue to receive his benefits. But it is still the case that if a person is out of work basically because of illness there is no benefit for him. This, as I say, is a most glaring gap in the social legislation of this country, and we urge the Government to act on this matter at an early date.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, there are still many items in our cupboard which we hope the Government will take and act upon at this session, and I urge in particular that this session not be prorogued until we have at least got the Canada Assistance Plan on the statute books.
I said I wanted to talk mainly about the procedures of Parliament. There is a paragraph in the Speech from the Throne the opening sentence of which reads as follows:
My ministers believe that it is imperative to reform the procedures of the House of Commons in order that it may accomplish the large volume of work required to meet the needs of the Canadian people in modern times.
We may find ourselves in some disagreement with the Government, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to ways and means of implementing that sentiment, but we could not agree with it more than we do. When it comes to improving the procedures of Parliament there are, of course, many items to be studied. There are many rules that need to be modernized, and even after we have looked at all the rules and made them the best they can be made, that is not everything. There is still room for reforming ourselves
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Knowles and for introducing those measures of selfdiscipline that will enable us to make this Parliament the place the people of Canada believe it is, the place they think it ought to be.
But I want to say that in terms of procedure, in terms of our rules, I think the most important problem that faces us-and it is alluded to in the sentence in the Speech from the Throne which I just read-is the problem of time. This is an age in which there have been all kinds of explosions that we hear about and read about. In Parliament in recent years we have had an explosion in the amount of business with which we have to deal, and unless we find some way to apportion, to allocate, to plan the use of our Parliamentary year we are going to find ourselves failing as a Parliament to serve the needs of the Canadian people.
Years ago when Parliament first met the year had 12 months and Parliament needed only a few of them to get the business done. Even this Government has not found it possible to provide more than 12 months in the year, and the last Government was not able to do so either. But we now seem to have enough business every year to take 15 or 20 months, and I suggest that poses a very direct problem and that we have to do something about planning and allocating the use of our time.
Lest it be thought that those of us who make statements like this are just generalizing, may I put one or two bits of statistics on the record. It is one of my hobbies not to read detective stories but to read Parliamentary documents. I hear some of my colleagues questioning my choice of reading matter but at any rate, Mr. Speaker, I find it a very interesting hobby. I find that back in the first two or three decades of the Parliament of Canada the sessions lasted two, two and a half or three months. Indeed there was not a single session prior to the turn of the century that reached a duration of four months. Even in World War I, when Canada grew up and became a nation amongst the nations of the world and dealt with terrific problems, the sessions lasted from four to four and a half months and no longer.
There was one session prior to World War I, the session of 1912-13, which is still referred to by oldtimers. I hope Senator Grattan O'Leary will not mind if I include him in that category because he has referred to it as a session that lasted almost as long as the last session of this House. But even that

session, which had the naval aid bill to deal with, which had the introduction of closure and the terrific battle it provoked, lasted from start to finish only six and a half months, and during that period of six and a half months there were two recesses.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Some of us in this chamber today were here during the sessions of World War II. We recall that during World War II Parliament was kept in session on a year round basis; from start to finish was a full calendar year. However, the actual number of weeks that we were in session was such that the sessions did not extend over six or six and a half months.
The facts are clear, Mr. Speaker. Down to the end of World War II, time was not a problem. The rules, I suggest, were made back in the days 100 or 200 years ago when time was not an issue, so arrangements were not necessary to plan the use of time. After all, if the nation's business at the federal level could be done in two and a half or three months, it was an avocation for those who came here, it was a prestigious position to be a Member, and the going was fairly easy. There needed to be no time limit on speeches; there needed to be no set adjournment time. Members just got things done in their own sweet way.
However, Mr. Speaker, all that has now changed. Today if we are going to deal with the tremendous amount of business that faces us we have to cope with the problem of time. In those early days Parliament dealt with such things as postal services, customs, railways and canals, but not many more things. Today everything that affects our people from the cradle to the grave, at home and abroad or in outer space, is the concern of Parliament. At each and every session the new events of the complicated life of the twentieth century impinge upon our jobs as Members of Parliament. It is this explosion in the amount of business that we have to do, the mounting accumulation of work that is ours, that faces us with the necessity of taking a look at the way we use our time.
There are some who would cut the Gordian knot by simply imposing rigid time limits and settling it in that way. I think it has to be faced that unless as a Parliament, unless as Members in all parties, we think about this and come to some kind of reasonable agreement, one of these days some Government with a majority is going to do that and do damage to Parliament in the process.
April 13, 1965	COMMONS
Those who would do it in that way, who would fix rigid time limits for everything, seem to take the position that the only job we have is to reach decisions, to vote, to pass the laws that are placed before us.
However, I suggest that our job in Parliament is twofold. It is, on the one hand, the making of decisions, the voting; but it is also, to put it plainly, to talk. The very word Parliament describes this institution as what it is and implies that the whole democratic process involves the taking of decisions after there has been a full and free discussion. Those are our two jobs; to talk, to discuss, to review matters thoroughly on the one hand, and to take votes, to reach decisions, on the other. The whole problem, the whole history of Parliamentary procedure, has been an attempt to find a balance between these two roles. Without free speech, without a guarantee that nothing will be done in undue haste, in fact without the right to look at a proposition in general and in detail, to do this a second and a third time, it would not be Parliament.
It is equally true that if the rules permit an endless expression of views to the point of preventing decisions from being taken, if so much time is spent on one or two matters that others do not get reached, then that too is not Parliament. Our undoubted responsibility is to protect the right of free speech in Parliament, but it is also our responsibility so to arrange our business, which is the public's business, that we deal with all of it each year.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when anyone talks about planning the Parliamentary year, about allocating time for debates, about making arrangements so that we move from one subject to another and get things done, there are those who say this is a denial of free speech. There are those who shout that awful word "closure". I want to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that no one in this House dislikes the closure rule that we now have on our books more than I do. I think it was conceived in sin and shapen in iniquity. It was brought in in the middle of a contentious debate and then applied to the debate that was already in process. Most of the times when it is applied this is done because the rules as they exist at the start of the debate fail to fit the situation. I do not believe the closure rule we have now works any better than would be the case if the referee in a football game tried to change the rules in the middle of the third quarter.
DEBATES	333
The Address-Mr. Knowles
As one who is against closure-indeed I voted against its use during the flag debate in the last session for the reasons I have just given, and for the reason that I think every time we use the present closure rule we put off the day when we will find a better way of coping with the problem of time-the point I want to make is this, that I think the deadliest form of closure we have in this Parliament is not the closure rule; is not the rule that says this Throne Speech debate shall last only eight days, the budget debate six days; is not the rule that prohibits Members from speaking more than a certain number of minutes. I think the deadliest form of closure is the practice of carrying some debates over so many days, so many weeks or so many months that we never get to the other important issues with which Parliament should be dealing.
I have criticized the Liberals over the years for their dilatory manner in bringing in the things they promised in 1919. I am still at it, still trying to get them to get along. However, even though a great deal of the fault lies in the fact that that is the Liberal way, it is true also that when you spend week after week on a flag debate, when you spend week after week on a pension plan that has been thoroughly gone into in a committee, you do not leave time to get at medicare, you do not leave time to get at the problems of Federal-Provincial relations and all the other tremendous problems now facing the people of Canada which should receive the attention of this Parliament. You cannot go on having a 14-month session every 12 months. What is serious about this is that in these 14-month sessions you have to spend so much time on a few subjects you do not get at the others. So, Mr. Speaker, as an opponent of closure- I mean the closure rule that is now on the books-I am equally opposed to the way in which Parliament has been spending so much time on some subjects that it has foreclosed the possibility of getting at some of the serious problems that face us in this House of Commons.
I say therefore that we should stop trying to deal with this question by using the word "closure", by saying it is a denial of free speech to plan our debates. It is no more a denial of free speech to say a certain debate shall last only a certain length of time than it is for you to say to me, Mr. Speaker, that I have only 30 minutes in this debate. If I try to go over 30 minutes, you will stop me. Is that closure against me? No; you are trying to
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Knowles protect the rights of other Members to speak as well. When we get to the point of planning important debates and reaching decisions after a time limit that has been agreed to, we will not be imposing closure, we will be protecting Parliament's right to get at other matters as well.
We had a suggestion today in a question by the hon. Member for Queens to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys of how the problems with which we have to deal in Parliament may multiply manyfold. We have problems now in dealing with Federal-Provincial relations, with social welfare, international relations, trade, and carrying on the war on poverty at home and abroad. If we have made contact with a civilization out in outer space, then we may need another secretary of state for external affairs more diplomatic than the one we have now. Our problems will multiply tremendously. When are we going to get time to deal with these problems if we do not plan and organize the use of the time we have? The hon. Member for Peace River suggests that there may need to be an ambassador to outer space.

speechtext:
Apparently there are more people being nominated for these posts than are willing to volunteer for them.
I would like to make the point that if we are going to go in for planning our Parliamentary year, for allocating the time that we use, we have to arrive at a means of doing it by agreement. This is where I am still asking questions about the Government's proposal. I read the opening sentence in the paragraph about this matter in the Speech from the Throne, and I agree with it 100 per cent. But the rest of that paragraph tells us the Government is going to bring proposals before Parliament in the field of procedure.
It is pretty hard to be critical of the Government at this point for doing this, because of the fact that we have moved pretty slowly in the matter of reforming the rules of the House; but we did make some progress last session, as a matter of fact a fair amount of progress. I do urge very strongly upon the Government, however, that it do not effect rule changes by having them brought in by the Government and passed directly on the basis of such majority as it can command.
I know the Government will say it is in a minority position, but it does seem to find support somewhere, sometimes by absentee-

ism, and it does seem to be able to put its will across. I suggest that rule changes imposed in that way will not work as well as rule changes arrived at by agreement among all parties in the House, and I suggest that if the Government has some proposals to lay before us it should keep this in mind.
I suggest there are some things that were agreed upon by the Special Committee on Procedure and Organization in the last session which did not get through the house, but which had the support of all the parties represented on that Committee, and the Government would be justified in finding a way to bring those measures before Parliament and give it a chance to vote on them one way or the other.
But if the Government has other proposals, for example something in the field of allocation of time, a rule that a subcommittee of mine worked out in the last session, its best course would be to present those proposals to the House and then have the House refer them to an all-party committee. It may take a little longer and I would not blame the Prime Minister for feeling a little impatient at the time it would take, but an agreement arrived at in that way will certainly work much better than something that bears the mark of having been imposed by the government of the day.
In entering this word of caution I am simply asking the Government to see to it that changing the rules is a job done by Parliament, not by the Government. Members of the Government found last session that in getting a flag through the House it became easier to do it when it was a parliamentary choice instead of a Government choice, and the same thing should apply to procedure. But even though I am entering this note of caution I am also urging the Government to find a way to get the House working on this matter.
We cannot go on year after year doing nothing about this problem of planning and allocating the use of our time, and I think we should get at it very early in this session. A good deal has been said about the many measures mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. Members of the House and newspapers are saying we will be here for another 14-month session, and we will be if we deal with all the measures contained in the Throne Speech as we ought to; but we are going to waste a lot of time if we do not cope with this main problem of time itself.
April 13, 1965

Therefore I urge the Prime Minister to bring whatever proposals the Government has in this field before the House. In so far as those proposals are ones that were already worked out last session by the Special Committee, I suggest it would be appropriate to ask the House to vote on them more or less right away. With respect to any other proposals I suggest they be referred immediately to another Special Committee on Procedure and Organization. Further, I suggest that Committee should work even harder than the Committee of last session, and having been a member of that last Committee I can say it worked very hard.
We should go into this matter with the clearcut realization that the people of Canada expect us to act on this important problem at this session of Parliament. To me, Mr. Speaker, a great deal is at stake, so far as democracy is concerned, in the image that Parliament has in the eyes of our people. We are being criticized, and I do not think there is anything wrong about the criticism we are subjected to in the press, over the radio and television. In fact, I think it is good for us. It would be tragic if the Canadian people were not paying any attention to us. It is good that they are discussing Parliament and, if you test Parliament by the amount of discussion about it, then this one stands up pretty well because we are certainly getting a lot of discussion. However, it is not good enough for us to bristle because we are being criticized. It not good enough for us to defend ourselves against the criticism. Our main response to it should be an attempt to improve things in Parliament itself.
As I have said, there are many rules, many details that can be looked at, and we must get at them. I have already said there is room for reforming ourselves, for improving our own self-discipline, but I think the most important problem is the use that we make of the Parliamentary year. The year still has only 12 months and I think it would be useful if some portion of those 12 months could be spent by Members in their constituencies. However, the main problem we have to cope with is finding how to allocate and use our time. I urge that it be on a planned basis. I urge it be on a basis of agreement. I think it can be worked out.
They have rules that cover this in other jurisdictions. We have worked out some things here, and I think if we feel the importance of this and have a bit of leadership from the Government on it, while at the same time it
Speaker's Ruling
is recognized that it is a parliamentary task, then we can do something about it.
I do not think the last rule of procedure will ever be written. Procedure in a free parliament is in fact living and dynamic. We will have to make other changes in the future to meet other needs that arise, but at this point in our history I believe what we need most are rules that will provide for agreement in advance on the allocation of time, so that in a common sense way we can get a year's business done inside a year, preferably with some time to spare so that Members can mingle a bit more with their constituents.
I have already made it clear that I do not propose a rigid time limit on everything. I do not propose rules that can be invoked without agreement among the various parties in the House. One must preserve the right to oppose to the ultimate when the Opposition feels that the Government is dead wrong, as the Liberals felt about the naval aid bill in 1913, and as most of us in the opposition felt about the pipe line bill in 1956. You do not have to worry about Parliament when extreme measures are introduced. Parliament will always rise in its own defence when the times demand it. Our problem is with the great and growing mass of routine business, and I believe if we are to achieve a balance between full discussion and getting things done, between latitude in debate and getting decisions made, we will have to plan our discussion time. This way, in my view, lies real freedom, freedom to discuss not just one issue but all the issues that present themselves to us, freedom not only to discuss but freedom to vote and to make decisions. This way, in my view, Parliament will survive.

speechtext:
The hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) rose this morning on a point of order when there was really nothing before the House. After listening to his long argument I stated I

April 13, 1965
Speaker's Ruling
would examine the matter and try to bring in a just decision this afternoon. I have since that time read the transcript and it appears to me that his objection is to item No. 9 which appears on today's Order Paper and which reads as follows:
That the recommendations contained in the report of the Prairie Farm Assistance Administration Commission of Enquiry, tabled on July 29, 1964, including the following two questions:
1.	Whether the permanent staff of the P.F.A.A. should be brought under the Civil Service Commission, and
2.	Whether there should be other changes in the operation of the P.F.A.A.,
be referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture and Colonization for such recommendations as it deems advisable.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I do not see that I have to go beyond the text of the resolution, which simply asks the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization, following the report of a Commission of Inquiry, to study that report including two questions, and make such recommendations as it deemed advisable. This is all, I respectfully submit, that is before the Chair, and on the face of it the resolution appears to be perfectly in order.
The hon. Member, however, suggests that I should go behind the resolution and he argues that the Government Order is a nullity and should be struck off the Order Paper. He also said that the Commission is not a judicial inquiry but that it is a Crown court without any appeal.
Points of order, according to citation 70 of Beauchesne are:
-questions raised with the view of calling attention to any departure from the Standing Orders of the customary modes of proceeding in debate, or in the conduct of legislative business-
I can see here no departure from the Standing Orders but rather a request that the Speaker decide what is purely a question of law and entirely outside his jurisdiction in relation to the powers of a commission of inquiry.
Citation 71(5) of Beauchesne states explicitly that:
The Speaker will not give a decision upon a constitutional question nor decide a question of law, though the same may be raised on a point of order or privilege.
This is exactly what happened. The hon. Member rose on a point of order and submitted to me what I consider to be a question of law, that is, whether the recommendations of the Commission of Inquiry are in excess of the powers and authorities granted to the Commissioner by the Governor in Council.

He wants me to declare those recommendations to be a breach of the Order in Council tabled in the Blouse of Commons and affixed to the report. He wants me further to declare those recommendations are null and void and of no force and effect.
If I were to decide this matter, I certainly would be going beyond the jurisdiction granted me by law and by the Standing Orders of this House. I would refer the House to an opinion of Mr. Deputy Speaker on October 25, 1963, with which I concur. In that case, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) had argued that a Bill should not be considered, that it was out of order because it was ultra vires the Parliament of Canada. The Deputy Speaker ruled, as reported at page 4036 for October 25, 1963 that:
-it should not be the responsibility of the Chair to rule whether a particular piece of legislation.. .is or is not within the competence of this House.
He then referred hon. Members to Standing Order 12 which limits and defines the duties and responsibilities of the Speaker, that is, to deciding on questions of order, not questions of law. The Deputy Speaker then quoted from page 825 of Beauchesne, third edition, which refers to a ruling of Hon. Lewis Wallbridge, Speaker, made on June 25, 1864, where he, the Speaker, stated:
That according to the usages of the British Parliament he was not bound to decide on a question of law.
Following that decision, I would also like to refer to citation 71(5) of Beauchesne, fourth edition, at page 61:
The Speaker will not give a decision upon a constitutional question nor decide a question of law, though the same may be raised on a point of order or privilege.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. B. Stewart (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) was educated in my constituency. The hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) had already displayed his reasoned approach to our nation's problems. It was no surprise therefore that, given their splendid topic, the speeches they delivered in the House commended themselves so highly to all Members. I wish to add my congratulations.
The Speech from the Throne is a rich document, but I want to concentrate this afternoon on two particular facets of the Speech. One of these concerns the Canada Assistance Plan and the other the plan for regional development. You will recall, Sir, that earlier this day the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for a report on the meeting that took place on April 8 and 9 between the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) and the welfare ministers for the Provinces. The Minister of National Health and Welfare could not remain this afternoon, but she has asked me to say some words on her behalf to discharge a responsibility in this regard.
The welfare ministers from all the ten provinces were present at this meeting, together with representatives from the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Developments in the field of welfare during the past year were discussed thoroughly and cordially. The major discussion at the meeting was on the proposed Canada Assistance Plan announced in the Speech from the Throne and outlined by the Prime Minister last Tuesday. I am happy to be able to report, on behalf of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, that the plan was given general approval by
April 13, 1985

the Provincial Ministers, who welcomed it as providing a basis for a more flexible approach to public welfare in Canada.
The plan in general conforms to the suggestions which had been made by the Provinces at previous conferences. It does not interfere with the right of the Provinces to continue the present assistance programs for the aged, the blind, and the disabled. Under the Canada Assistance Plan recipients will be granted assistance on the basis of their needs. The plan will extend Federal cost-sharing to needy mothers, to the health costs of recipients and to expenditures for improved administration of assistance programs and welfare services for recipients.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
During the conference the Minister went into somewhat more detail than was possible earlier. First, she made it clear that Canada is prepared to match dollar for dollar the expenditures that the provinces now make in the field of mothers' allowances, that is, aid to mothers with dependant children. Second, the Minister explained that Canada is now prepared to share in the costs of health services provided by the Provinces to public assistance recipients. Under this proposal provision is made for the inclusion of the costs of medical, nursing, dental and optical care and drugs. The extent that such services cover will be for the Provinces themselves to decide, and it will be up to them to make the types of arrangements for the provision of health services that they consider most suitable in their particular case. In her discussions with the Welfare Ministers, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) also made very clear, as did the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) himself last Tuesday, that the health proposal is an interim measure which will carry on only until the medicare program comes into operation, which the Minister hopes will be very soon.
Another important feature of the plan which was warmly received by the Provincial Ministers of Welfare was the one calling for a sharing in new expenditures for the expansion of staff and services. This proposal recognizes the need for increased and better trained public assistance staffs to make possible a rehabilitative approach through lowering case loads, through adjustment of the requirements of assistance recipients, and through referral to training, employment, medical, and other resources. It is anticipated
The Address-Mr. Stewart many of those now receiving assistance can attain independence. Sir, I should hope that the aspect of the Speech from the Throne which was discussed at this meeting, which took place last Thursday and Friday, is one to which the House will be able to turn rapidly, once we have completed the debate on the Budget.

speechtext:
I will inquire about this, Mr. Speaker, to ascertain if such papers as were used at the conference could be presented. This might cause some difficulty, as you would realize I am sure, because it may be that the Provinces would not wish a portion of the documentation to be revealed when other parts were not.
I think perhaps I will go on with the other aspect of the Speech from the Throne with which I wanted to deal this afternoon. The other aspect of the Speech from the Throne to which I wish to direct attention this afternoon concerns the plans for regional development. As you perhaps remember, Sir, there has been some disputation in this House recently about to whom Nova Scotians should give thanks for certain economic improvements in their Province. This dispute was predictable because both Governments, the Government of Canada and the Government of Nova Scotia, have been active, and it is far from easy to sort out the credits.
The truth-no matter to whom the praise or blame as the case may be should go-is that unemployment in Nova Scotia is much too high. The release made on March 17, 1965 on the condition of the labour force shows that while on February 20, 1965, approximately 20,000 more persons were employed in the Atlantic region than one year earlier, the unemployment rate was 13 per cent. In every other region of Canada, there had been a decline in the unemployment rate during that period, but in the Atlantic region it had gone up from 12.7 per cent in February, 1964, to 13 per cent in February, 1965. It is encouraging to learn from the Speech from the Throne that this Government is keenly aware of this regional problem and is devising measures to cope with it.
In 1956, when the Bill that eventually was to become the Area Redevelopment Act was before the Senate of the United States, a

April 13, 1965
The Address-Mr. Stewart sharp disagreement became evident between the views of two very distinguished Senators who participated in the debate. One was Senator Goldwater and the other was Senator John F. Kennedy. Actually there was an element of truth in what both said. Speaking on July 25, 1956, Mr. Goldwater said:
The whole history of this country's development refutes the contention of those who would invoke extreme federal remedies in such situations. In the West, for instance, we have experienced the boom development of certain areas, only to realize, at some later date when the economic sources were dissipated, the collapse of whole communities which exist today only as ghost towns. During such transitions, our people did not seek governmental assistance for the artificial stimulation of areas whose economic wells had run dry. They accepted the tribulations of their ventures with stout hearts and strong backs, just as in the beginning they accepted their triumphs.
It is clear that Senator Goldwater was thinking almost exclusively about primary industries based on some scarce natural resource. This being recognized, we must concede that there is some validity in what he said. If the industries that maintain a population are based on gold, timber, oil or some similar resource, and if these are exhausted and no other economic base is introduced, there is no point in trying to maintain new generations in that place.
Senator Kennedy, speaking earlier that same day, contended that:
-the responsibility of the federal government to aid such areas is commonly acknowledged. This responsibility is in the interest of the areas which are subject to chronic unemployment and underemployment, and coincides also with the interests of the nation. The fact is that these less fortunate areas exert a general drag upon the economy and the federal government, in order to assure full prosperity for the nation as a whole, should do all it can to eliminate pockets of unemployment and underemployment.
It is quite clear that Senator Kennedy was thinking of people engaged in secondary and tertiary industries. There are limits beyond which a country such as Canada should not go in efforts to help less fortunate areas, because to go beyond those limits would be to endanger the nation's position in the international market. On the other hand, as Senator Kennedy was insisting, such areas, if permitted to exist for long, exact their price. They do constitute a drag on regional prosperity and on the national economy as well. I think we can say safely that if either Senator Goldwater's position or Senator Kennedy's position was pushed in practice to its extreme, the result would be very costly. The Goldwater extreme would
[Mr. Stewart.!
promote complete population mobility; that is, it would allow economic causes freely to move the population to the favoured national sites of secondary and tertiary industry. The extreme Kennedy position is to accept population stagnation, that is, to try to bring employment to all the people wherever they live.
Now, these distinctions are relevant to the identification of the areas to which measures for regional development are to apply. The general conclusion to which we are driven by them is that if special measures for regional economic development are to be effective, unless we are dealing with primary industries based on a local resource, the smaller the areas selected the more expensive the measures that will be effective. The area development program, which now provides tax incentives taking the form of a three-year income tax exemption and accelerated write-offs of the capital costs of both machinery and equipment and new buildings acquired by new manufacturing and processing enterprises has been helpful in Nova Scotia, for example, in attracting new industries to places like Canso, Abercrombie, Stellarton, and Point Edward. The areas eligible for these incentives have been those national employment service areas wherein there has been relatively high unemployment. The Speech from the Throne reveals that the Government is now proposing to expand its program to include other areas where incomes are low.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
This is encouraging. We know that the National Employment Service areas are only administrative areas. As labour market areas they can be regarded as sufficiently distinct to serve as the long-run theatres for economic development programs only if we forget that population mobility, not population stagnation, is essential to the reformation of the economy of the Atlantic region. A program of regional development directed at the Atlantic Provinces must deal, not with mere administrative units but with genuine economic regions.
It is desirable, of course, to employ statistical criteria in identifying the less fortunate areas. Without such criteria the Government will find itself involved in highly subjective judgments and would be subject to heavy local pressures. But it is also desirable to assure that the areas selected are justifiable in terms of their economic potential for either primary, resource-based industries or for secondary and tertiary industries. Other-
April 13, 1965	COMMONS DEBATES	341
The Address-Mr. Stewart
wise, the measures applied will be either relatively ineffectual or extremely costly.
What I am proposing is that while statistical criteria should be used to ascertain the localities in which the population is plagued by high unemployment and low incomes, the special development measures should not be restricted to those localities, but should be applied to the general economic region in which such localities prevail. I am suggesting that the regional development policy ought to be based on a recognition that the most promising growth centres, even if now relatively prosperous, must not be excluded from growth encouragement. Do not cast your seeds on only the rocky ground! Perhaps, Sir, at this juncture I ought to mention that my entire constituency is already eligible for tax incentives under the designated area program, so I am not pleading my own case.
In addition to forecasting a new method for defining the regions needing development, the Speech from the Throne forecasts both new measures "to aid industrial expansion" in those regions and measures "to help people to take full advantage of such improved employment opportunities."
It has been known all along that the present tax incentive program for designated areas has not been regarded by the Government as a full-blown program for regional development. I think we may conclude from the Speech from the Throne that the Government is now ready to put into effect a new and higher phase of its program. Just what the new measures to aid industrial expansion will be we cannot say at this time, but I would presume they will not include any plan to transmit Federal money to the Provinces, to be used by the Provinces to provide direct proportional grants toward either the capital costs or the payroll costs of new ventures. Any such plan would entail many difficulties.
There are certain advantages for all concerned when a training program is established for the potential employees of projected industry. I assume it is some such training program that the Government has in mind in this laconic passage in the Speech from the Throne. Men and women could be recruited from near and far according to their potentialities for the projected work, and trained specifically for that work. In this way the training program would not simply take in the people who happen to arrive at the technical or vocational school's door. I hope this is what is forecast in the paragraph to which I have just referred.
It is encouraging to note that reference is made in the Speech from the Throne to the ARDA program. In the Atlantic Provinces the ARDA program is the other side of the coin of development. It is most important that our land resources be used properly, whether the use to which they are put be agriculture, forestation, or recreation. I have a feeling, Mr. Speaker, that in some of our Provinces the possibilities of the ARDA program are not thoroughly appreciated. We get small projects, important perhaps to some Minister or to some locality, but projects which by being small create the image of the ARDA program as a rather dreary undertaking.
The ARDA program ought to be approached most imaginatively; and I say that, realizing that large parts of my constituency being underdeveloped have, in the very fact that they are underdeveloped, great potentiality.
Back in 1957, in the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects, there was set forth a paragraph which I will abbreviate as follows:
An objective of economic policy should be to integrate and improve the basic economic framework of the Atlantic region, including in particular the transportation facilities of the area, with a view to facilitating and encouraging economic growth within the region. This is not likely to be accomplished by a multiplicity of unco-ordinated measures providing aid on an ad hoc basis. . . What is needed we believe is bold comprehensive and co-ordinated approach to the underlying problems of the region in order to make the best possible use of the resources of the area and to improve transportation and other basic services.
I am glad that the Government has remembered that passage in the report of the Gordon Royal Commission. There is a great danger in all unco-ordinated approaches to economic development, particularly when two, or even three levels of government assume some responsibility for that development.
One of the complaints we have been hearing in Atlantic Canada recently is that there are so many agencies for regional development, both Federal and Provincial, that it is difficult not only to understand the distinct undertakings of each of the several agencies but even to remember what the initials of their names stand for. I should hope that the proposed special Federal-Provincial conference would help in clarifying the goals of these various agencies and in harmonizing federal and provincial policies and programs.
In this connection I should like to suggest that when the general Federal-Provincial conference on regional development has finished
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Stewart its work, there should be a special session involving the Government of Canada and the Governments of the four Atlantic Provinces, because I think that certain of the problems germane to the discussion that would take place at such a conference would not be directly relevant to other parts of the country. Such a conference, if well planned, could be most helpful in producing a better understanding between the Provinces and the Government of Canada, and in shaping the kinds of policies which will be necessary.
In this kind of venture organization is very important. One of the most encouraging aspects of the Speech from the Throne is that the Prime Minister himself is proposing to direct his own attention to this assault upon regional economic stagnation. In the Atlantic Provinces, as you might expect, we have a great deal of confidence in the Prime Minister, and that in itself is important.

speechtext: Speak for yourself, John.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, we do have certain people who disagree, but such ones are always with us. What is even more important, Sir, is that the inevitable temptation for different agencies to go their several ways can be overcome if the Prime Minister himself is directly involved. The future development of the Atlantic region is going to require the co-operation of the Federal Department of Public Works, the Federal Department of Transport, the Federal Department of Finance, the Federal Department of Industry, the Federal Department of Labour, and the Atlantic Development Board. If all these agencies are going to work harmoniously together without dispersion of energy and conflict of interest, without the leadership of the Prime Minister nothing much will be accomplished. That is why I am glad that the Government has resisted the temptation, an almost inevitable temptation, I suppose, to set up a ministry for regional development. That would have been a mistake. What is needed is the ordinary departmental approach to this problem, co-ordinated by the Minister whose job it is to co-ordinate the works of the several departments, namely the Prime Minister.
There is one other topic to which I want to refer very briefly, Sir, in conclusion. It is a related topic, for unless something is done about it and unless it is taken seriously neither the Canada Assistance Plan nor the plan for

regional development will ever find their way, via the statute books, into action. I refer to the need for reform of our procedures in this House, a subject which was discussed earlier this afternoon by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I think it would be a mistake to found a demand for parliamentary reform on the experience-experience which extended to some 248 days, it is true-of the last session of this Parliament. But we all know, and it has been known since the days of World War II, that this House and its Committees seldom work intensively enough on the increasingly large bulk of public business which comes before them. Too much time is spent in what one might call the parliamentary doldrums.
The Special Committee on Procedure established last session at the instigation of the Government worked earnestly and long for basic reform, but we know the sorry reward of their efforts. I think it is now quite clear that nothing much could be achieved to reform our procedures unless the Government itself acts. It is encouraging to see in the Speech from the Throne that the Government does propose to undertake specific reforms essential to parliamentary reform. As the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre said, there are two aspects to this. We are here to discuss, and we are here to decide. The reconciliation of these two aims, which are likely to be viewed rather differently according to where one sits in this House, is not easy; but it is now patently clear that no solution more satisfactory than the one we now have, which is to experience something like a 14 or 15 month session, is likely to be attained unless the Government itself goes ahead, assumes the responsibility for proposing necessary reforms, and brings those reforms forward for debate, and, in good time, to a decision in this House.

I would be less than gracious were I not also to include in my congratulations and compliments the hon. Member for Westmorland (Mrs. Rideout) on her maiden speech. She discussed Maritime union, which has been discussed in the Maritimes for all of 110 years. Her interest is in locating the capital of such a union, of such a country or new province, which might be called Acadia, in Moncton.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I prefer a different approach. I would think it would be better for the time being that the capital rotate between St. John's, Newfoundland, Halifax, Charlottetown and Fredericton, and then in the millennium we can come to Moncton.
However, now we have solved the problems of Maritime union I would like to pass on to a problem that the Principal and ViceChancellor of McGill, Dr. Robertson, calls really the crisis in the country today. He says that the "developing crisis in higher education" ranks as a national problem second only to "the problem of unity in our country".
That was in a speech reported in the Montreal Star of April 5. The Vice-Chancellor of York University in the United Kingdom, Lord James of Rusholme, says that the Federal Government must put education higher on its priorities list. I would think most of us in this House, no matter what our political affiliation, would agree with Lord James of Rusholme.

speechtext:
We will deal with where I stand in a moment. I am disappointed in the Speech from the Throne because it has not faced the crisis of higher education in any manner. I think the problem of assistance to universities is, as Dr. Robertson said, the second most important thing in this country. The other day in Fredericton, New Brunswick, 1,500 students met before the Legislative
April 13, 1965

The Address

Mr. Fairweather Assembly of that Province protesting the increase in fees of the University of New Brunswick at Mount Allison. Then in the other two universities that I know of, which have increased their fees, Acadia and Dal-housie, similar protests have been made to Government. Many years ago in the United States a group of researchers, academics and practising lawyers formed what is known as the Law Institute, which from time to time prepares and publishes a brief restatement of a particular aspect of the law. For example, there is the restatement of the law on torts, on practice, on evidence, and so on. The Institute does this because changing conditions demand different solutions for problems, different concepts and different approaches.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, it is time that a group of Canadians with an interest in and concern for the rapidly developing crisis in higher education prepared just such a restatement of the constitutional concept of the word "education" as used in the British North America Act. The Federal Government, in spite of several well documented briefs from the Canadian Universities Foundation, plus innumerable individual requests, has done nothing to change the formula for per capita grants for universities since the Diefen-baker Government increased these grants from $1.50 to $2 effective June 1, 1962. The university operating budgets have far outstripped the increase in population and the $2 per capita figure, in order that it be in any way comparable with present day buying power should be a minimum of $2.95. I presume that is where my hon. friend from Danforth (Mr. Scott) got his $3 figure yesterday.
