speechtext:
The hon. Member says he was just rounding it out. Well, the nickel would be very helpful. The actual federal per capita grants to universities as of June 1 this year will be about $39,300,000, whereas if the grants had kept pace with the increase in university operating costs-that is, $2.95 per capita-they would be approximately $58 million. I suggest this is a substantial difference, and it is a difference that should make hon. Members who support the Government just a little bit ashamed of that Government's neglect of higher education in this country.
The problem is not, however, simply one of dollars for university operating grants. The restatement I seek is for a co-ordinated


approach by Federal and Provincial Governments to special aspects of higher education, but within the framework and basic philosophy of the Constitution. I think this can be done. I think there are people in, say the Province of Quebec and on the Treasury benches, who could re-negotiate this matter of education in so far as the Constitution is concerned.
Some aspects of higher education which recognize neither Provincial nor, for that matter, national boundaries are, I suggest, in the areas of research, overseas students and programs involving studies of the cultures of lands other than our own. For example, Canada's needs for nuclear physicists cannot be circumscribed by the statutory injunction making education solely a provincial responsibility. Researchers in medicine and in the dynamics of space flights will not be impressed by a narrow and restrictive constitutional debate. McGill University, in its most excellent brief to the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, put it this way:
There are two major dimensions to the role of a modem university. The first is universality. Language, culture, and social milieu are factors that influence the quality and style of its activities, but to be worthy of the designation "university", it must have a commitment to the quest for knowledge that transcends these particulars. The second dimension is is involvement in the society of which it is a part. The role of educational institutions generally is to nourish and develop the culture of the society in which they exist and which they serve.
The changing circumstances of the twentieth century have altered the character of the university and changed its role but they have increased, rather than diminished, its interests and responsibilities beyond the margins of the immediate community in which it finds itself.
It is in this context, then, that I seek a new accord between the Government of Canada and the Provincial Governments in the field of higher education while ensuring academic freedom and preserving fundamental provincial rights. Let Canada as a nation develop a sophisticated formula for ensuring that the universities of this land can provide us with the necessary number of doctors and scientists for our national needs and our international obligations. This type of accord, it seems to me

and I am not going to talk for very long about it-was found in another area of largely provincial concern, and that is of natural resources, in the conference held in Montreal a couple of months ago, the Resource Conference. It is this type of approach that I think could well be used in the field of education.
April 13, 1365

Let Canada assist some of our great universities establish schools of Asian and of African studies, for example. Then, too, we could have a Foreign Service Institute which, I suggest, could transfuse the Departments of External Affairs, Trade and Commerce and other Government Departments with qualified recruits. I feel that there is a mood prevalent in both French and English speaking Canada for a redrawing of the present too restrictive areas of responsibility in the field of education. Let us harness the mood, restate the principles and give university education, particularly at the graduate level, a clear direction for what I think of as the exciting years ahead.
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the New Democratic Party outlined various projects for higher education. I think it was a pity that they could not wait to announce them-they have all been busy with election manifestos here; the Throne Speech, and now the New Democratic Party on higher education-in August of this year, when we expect to have the results of the Bladen Commission report on higher education. I think this is something of an indication of our constitutional thin skin in the fact that the Canadian Universities Foundation found the money and the formula for this Commission, which the Government of Canada, because of a narrow concept of education, could not finance, or for which it could not provide the initiative.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
As you know, Dr. Vincent Bladen, the Chairman, who is Dean of Arts and Sciences at the University of Toronto; Dr. Louis Paul Dugal, Dean of Pure and Applied Sciences; Hon. Senator W. W. McCutcheon and Mr. Howard Ross of the well-known firm Touche, Ross, Bailey and Smart, are Commissioners studying the financing of higher education in Canada. Not only are they studying it, but they are to make recommendations on the financing of universities and colleges in Canada, with particular reference to the decade ending in 1975, respecting financial requirements of universities and colleges for operation, research, physical facilities and student aid. They are also studying the proportion of the financial support of higher education which should be provided by tuition fees, contributions from governments, corporations, foundations and individuals. They are studying policies regarding the allocation of funds for higher education, and criteria by which institutions and students should be deemed eligible to receive such aid.
The Address[DOT]-Mr. Fairweather
I am sure the recommendations of this Commission will be watched by the Government of Canada in spite of the fact that at the moment there is no co-ordination of this field. I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) some time ago who had replaced Dr. Taylor in the Privy Council office, and who was to advise the Government in this area. I have not received an answer as yet, and I do not know whether or not it means that nobody has replaced Dr. Taylor.
There is a serious gap in Federal responsibility, and I think it is no longer good enough just to slough off responsibility by rushing to Section 93 of the Constitution, which was drafted years ago when colleges were just local colleges and had not conceived of the universality which the McGill Commission submission so eloquently set out.
There are one or two other things I should like to mention in the field of higher education. One is the suggestion of the Canadian Universities Foundation in respect of national achievement awards. These awards would be made in the form of remissions of portions of loans made under the Canada Student Loans Fund. There would be remissions made if students achieved superior marks. This is the type of challenge for excellence that we in Parliament should encourage. I think this would be much better than grinding out loans without any thought as to how well the students receiving the loans are doing.
Another interesting suggestion which I certainly cannot claim as my own, but one chat I had the opportunity of passing on, is that a national university be established on the site which will be vacated some day when Expo '67 completes its exposition. This would certainly be a good location because it would have the advantage of utilizing the two founding cultures in Canada.
Another problem we must face in respect of higher education is created by the lack of real, meaningful exchange programs between students of French Canada and those of so-called English Canada. This could be encouraged in a much more massive way than is taking place now.
We have had some discussion here about the rules of this House. It was my privilege to serve on the House Committee on Organization and Procedure. I have not been here for very long, but that was the high mark certainly for me during my two years in Parliament. I sometimes think in respect of

The Address-Mr. Fairweather the matter of Parliamentary rules that we worship the form but forget the substance. I think it is time we considered the substance and ignored the form. I have had 10 years experience in a small Provincial Legislature, if I may become personal for a moment, and I have followed the happenings in Legislatures of other Provinces. I can assure the House that these small Provincial Legislatures go through about ten times the amount of work, in about half the time, as we do here. I think it is incumbent upon us as Members of Parliament to do something about this situation. I welcome that part of the Throne Speech, to which I will give enthusiastic support when it comes before us in the form of legislation.
It has been said here this afternoon that the House of Commons is a dynamic place. If this need be said anywhere else, let me remind hon. Members that people have been talking about this and writing about it to a great degree, particularly because we are now celebrating the 700th anniversary of Parliament as an institution. Obviously rules and procedures have undergone tremendous changes during that 700-year period; but sometimes sitting here I wonder whether during some of the debate we are not living the whole 700 years of history. That of course is another story.
Because this is a Speech which has not been carefully typed and prepared, I must take a moment or two to consult my notes. This seems to be about the right juncture to discuss for just a moment what I envisage as a division, if I may call it that, of the roles of a Member of Parliament. Some of us forget that we are really three people in one, with three separate roles. The first role surely is to represent the people of our constituencies. I suggest this is only one role, but a very important one, and one which cannot be forgotten or, if forgotten, at the peril of each Member.
The second role is one of obligation as an educator in our ridings and throughout the country. The last role of a Member of Parliament embodies an obligation to the country to give it "his unbiased opinion, his mature judgment and his enlightened conscience." Edmund Burke said so in 1774, and it seems to me that his affirmation of that day still stands.
It is in this context that I want to speak about a problem which I face as a representative, as an educator, as well as one who has a duty to give an unbiased opinion. It troubles me to think that the Royal Commission on Biculturalism and Bilingualism is touching only the high spots. By that, Sir, I mean the

large centres of population in this country. In spite of the efforts of the mass media to get the message across, I do not believe the results of this Commission's work are reaching the small towns, villages and countrysides of Canada. This is a serious defect in the work of this Commission. I am one of those individuals who believes, and this is almost too trite to mention, that hate and prejudice are not inherited but are taught. Surely this is a role for this Royal Commission. It is all very well to hear briefs at the King Edward Hotel in Toronto, but I wonder whether the Commission could not fragmentize itself and hear briefs at the Queen's Hotel at Sussex, New Brunswick, which has a population of 2,500. I think it is only by hearing the type of message that might come from small communities of this kind that this Commission will find out what the general public thinking is.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I have been intrigued, as any Canadian must be, by the sensible thoughts of Dr. Wilder Penfield. He says, of course, that in teaching other languages our fault is that we start too late. I have always wondered why some Canadians sneer at those who have the privilege of having a second or third language. In Europe and in fact almost anywhere in the world but in North America this would be taken for granted. Yet I am afraid that in Canada we have not yet reached that stage in our civilizing process when second and third languages are taken in this matter of fact way. I know this is not particularly a Federal field, but undoubtedly the Bilingualism and Biculturalism Commission will be giving attention to how the teaching of the second language can begin, not in secondary school but in kindergarten.
I think that is about all I have to say, except for one last point. Yesterday the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan, posed a question to which a good many writers and thinkers have been giving their attention lately. I refer to the fact that so much of government at the present time is taking place outside the forum of this Parliament, and in fact in the forums of the Legislatures, in committee rooms in the West Block and in committee rooms in hotels across this land; and unless this type of thing is stopped we as members are going to put ourselves out of business, so to speak. Many people might think this is a good idea. Claude Ryan, writing the other day in Le Devoir, pointed out that there are eight fields in the Speech from the Throne that will require
April 13, 1S65

Dominion-Provincial conferences or Canada-Provincial conferences, or whatever the new, modern, up to date word is for "dominion". I think we have to be very careful that this type of conference is exposed to proper, public debate and criticism, which can only take place either in this Parliament or in a Legislature.
I support the Canada Pension Plan; but let me cite it as an example. It troubled me to think that the plan could not really be changed at all and that the debate here was in effect a sham, because all decisions had already been made. The excuse was given that matters had all been cleared up or clarified, or that an agreement had been made with the Provinces; and we were left more or less to put "well done" on the document and shoot it off to the Senate.
We are going to be considering very soon another very important piece of legislation involving the patriation of the Constitution- which is not a patriation at all, because the constitution, of course, will remain a United Kingdom statute. But it would be very disturbing if those on the treasury benches came to us-in fact, as Members of Parliament we cannot let it happen-and said to us: There is nothing you can do or say now because it has all been agreed to long ago by the Legislatures of the Provinces, or has been the subject of some agreement. I do not care whether it is the Fulton formula, the Favreau formula, the Fulton-Favreau formula or some other combination of names that it is currently popular to attach to it. I want to see the formula.
I support the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). I think the proper place to examine the matter is in a committee and I certainly think the very fullest debate must be held on this problem. It would be an absolute negation of all our responsibilities if we were to be told that we would have no opportunity to change the formula or to amend the philosophy, and so on, just because the Legislatures had done something. This is a field on which the political scientists I see sitting on the other side of the House can put their classes to work for years to come. I sort of think of it as a nonparliamentary process, with everything being nicely tied up and handed to us, and with our not having an opportunity to examine the matter thoroughly.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I should like to congratulate the hon. Member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) on his very thought-provoking and moderate speech. While I do not agree with all portions of his speech, or with all his opinions I do share his desire for peace and unity in this nation and I most certainly subscribe to the teachings of Dr. Penfield which, if they were implemented a little more fully, I think would do much to make bilingualism a reality.
Tradition affords me the opportunity to congratulate the hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) on their contributions to the debate on the Speech from the Throne. The spontaneous applause and many messages of congratulations sent their way indicate the respect of all Members, regardless of political affiliation, for well-prepared and well-delivered speeches. Perhaps what is even more important, this is an indication of the bond of affection that does at times permeate and traverse traditional partisan lines, although in modern times I think that the bond of affection has perhaps too often been buried in the rubble of political partisanship.
The reaction in the House to the Speech from the Throne is, I think, traditional in that we on the Government side indicate what we like about it and those in the Opposition indicate what is missing. But I have been rather pleased at the reception that the proposed legislation set forth in the Speech from the Throne has received in leading editorials in our large daily newspapers. I do not intend to read from these editorials, but in a general way I believe they come to the conclusion that the Speech from the Throne does indicate a determination on the part of the Liberal Party to continue to implement the type of social welfare measures
April 13, 19G5

The Address-Mr. Mackasey that Canadians of this day and age have come to expect from the Liberal Party. But underlying the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, is an awareness of the fact that all our welfare measures must be paid for by an ever-expanding economy, one that will provide the jobs for newcomers to the labour market, one that will provide positions for those who must be retrained to new skills, and an economy that must provide the moneys not only for social welfare measures but also for the new legislation that is contemplated in the Speech from the Throne. I would say to my good friends from the N.D.P. who were talking about our constant borrowing from the cupboard, that if all the social welfare measures suggested in the Throne Speech are implemented their cupboard would bear a great similarity to Mother Hubbard's.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
One thing that appealed to me in the Throne Speech, Mr. Speaker, was the reestablishment of a Special Committee of the House of Commons known as the Food and Drugs Committee. The purpose as outlined in the Throne Speech will be specifically to aim at reducing the prices paid by the public for drugs. While the Throne Speech is by nature rather sketchy in detail, I would have hoped that the reference to the price of drugs would have been tied in with some reference to the necessity for maintaining, above all else, that degree of safety that we in Canada have come to expect from our pharmaceutical manufacturers, and which I have come to realize more and more, as an active member of that Food and Drugs Committee, has a direct bearing on the cost of drugs, as do the moneys being spent on research and the construction of more and more research laboratories.
It is imperative, Mr. Speaker, that the cost of drugs to the Canadian public be as low as possible, consistent with our Canadian ideas of free enterprise, the realization of safety standards established by the Food and Drugs Directorate, and compatible with the development and expansion of our pharmaceutical manufacturing industry which, as at present in Montreal and Toronto, does provide thousands of jobs and money toward the almost disgraceful lack of pure research in this country.
The second significant paragraph in the Throne Speech alludes to the proposed legislation to strengthen the position of Canadian publications. While it is tempting, Mr. 
Speaker, to comment at length on such proposed legislation, I would prefer to do so when the proposed legislation is before the House. But I do note with a great deal of interest the substitution of the word "publication" for "periodical". This coincides with an opinion I expressed in the House almost a year ago, that when Canada loses complete control in the field of communications, radio programs, television, newspapers and magazines, then the day will have arrived when Canada ceases to grow as a nation. My sentiments cannot and must not be regarded as anti-American but rather as pro-Canadian. I submit there is a fundamental difference. I believe it is imperative that our daily newspapers remain in full control of Canadians; that our editorials in those daily newspapers remain in the hands of Canadians, Canadians who can interpret the events in this House and in this country, as well as international affairs, free from the natural bias that could prevail in those editorials if they originated from some other source outside of this nation. I would urge the Government, Mr. Speaker, to introduce this legislation as soon as possible. The present uncertainty that prevails over the magazine field as a result of the ever present legislation on the Order Paper is unfair to those Canadian periodicals who look hopefully for some solution to their financial problem. It is unfair also to those periodicals under scrutiny, and as yet unaccepted as Canadian periodicals; who have the right to have their position defined once and for all so that they, too, may plan for their future, if there is one for them in Canada. I do not pretend to know the solution to the problem of the periodicals, but I do feel it is not in the best interest or not in the best Canadian tradition to retard appropriate legislation any longer. If it is undemocratic to introduce discriminatory retroactive legislation, then we must and should spell out correctly what this Government feels constitutes a Canadian publication.
The indication that this Government intends to go forward with its proposal to establish a Canadian Development Corporation to assist in financing major new industrial developments in this country, to increase the Canadian ownership of business corporations, reflects the determination of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to help reduce, by legislation if possible, the ever-continuing erosion of our own industries and of our industrial resources to foreign interests. It
April 13, 1965	COMMONS
indicates a type of Canadianism that is not as prevalent as it should be in certain financial circles. It is indeed a tribute to the Minister of Finance that he is willing to introduce ways and means that must cause some eyebrow lifting amongst his business acquaintances, with whom he was associated so long before he decided to serve his country through the medium of elected office.
If time permitted, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the officers of Power Corporation who recently showed enough initiative to take over Consolidated Paper, and with this takeover regain for this country control over a large tract of forest and natural resources as well, of course, as regaining control over Consolidated Paper's Canadian subsidiary. In a speech made recently in Winnipeg Maurice Strong, President of Power Corporation, advocated the establishment of more corporations similar in make-up and purpose to Power Corporation, corporations that would not hesitate to take over parent firms rather than seek out a minority voice in Canadian subsidiaries. This type of initiative, combined with the legislation to be introduced by the Minister of Finance establishing the Canadian Development Corporation, will do much to help us retain what is left of our Canadian identity in the business world.
I should have liked to continue in this vein, Mr. Speaker, because as a Member of the Government Party the opportunities to speak in the House are not as frequent as some of us would like. I, Mr. Speaker, rarely depart from this type of speech, rarely participate unless I feel I have something to say. Rarely do I take the time of the House to retaliate or answer personal attacks upon this Party or upon Members of this Party. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I share the opinion of a well-known United States congressman-I believe his name was Joe Cannon-who rose to be Speaker in the House of Representatives. One day he was asked why he did not retaliate to a rather vicious attack that had just been made and he replied. All this has no meaning to that limited section of the Conservative Party which includes the Horners and the Nielsens and is led by Mr. Diefen-baker. Member for seizing the opportunities provided by his propensity to destructiveness to push his way to the top of his party, to be the voice behind the Leader of the Opposition. ada that the Prime Minister is striving for, and the voice of the hon. Members who saw the program would have a great laugh at the expense of the Prime Minister. Well, I saw that program, Mr. Speaker, and I would defend the C.B.C.'s right to present it with my last breath, for I will never subscribe to censorship in any form. But this does not preclude me from saying that the program was in bad taste, that ridiculing the Prime Minister of this country, or for that matter ridiculing the President of the United States, indicates what many people have long suspected about this program, that it is running out of constructive and creative ideas, and is failing to live up to the high hopes many people had for it at its inception. Its reference to the flag as "the rag" is despicable and can only weaken the respect that all Canadians should have for our national symbol, regardless of the controversy that preceded its adoption. The same performers who imitated the Prime Minister, creating the impression that the Prime Minister may have referred to the flag as the rag and who in turn ridiculed the President of the United States, have no compunction about crossing the border to take advantage of the opportunities there for second rate comedians.

This Throne Speech covers the whole ambit of difficulties which exist today in Canada. I am not here making an election speech, but I am not worried about an election being called. You can call one at any time you wish, but this House should get down to business and bring forward legislation which does not need complete overhaul. Legislation brought forward by the present Government has required overhauling, and this has been carried out as a result of the efforts of Members on this side of the House. When that has taken place many of the newspapers in this country have suggested that the delay in passage is all Mr. Diefenbaker's fault. On the other side of the coin, the Government has continually accepted credit for the few measures which have not required overhaul.
As an example of what I have in mind, let me ask why the Pension Plan had to be submitted three times and is still, in my opinion, a failure. On many occasions we have not been given the opportunity to vote for or against certain programs, but have been put off by arguments as to whether or not we should have the right to discuss them at all. Let us have some positive discussions about the measures which this Government brings forward. Surely the time has come when we should return parliamentary powers to Parliament. Let us stop appointing Royal Commissions and creating Crown corporations to denude Parliament of its powers.
It was pleasing to me to note that the Government intends to at least suggest the appointment of an ombudsman. This points up the fact that there are many things wrong with the bureaucratic administration of this

country. I should also like to see an end to the creation of Crown corporations which presumably take the powers of administration out of the hands of Parliament, following which they can hide behind these administrative screens and refuse to accept responsibility.

On March 8 I stood in this House and asked the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) whether the Secretary of the Army Benevolent Fund had been suspended. He has been in charge of the Canadian Army Benevolent Fund as Secretary for 17 years. The Address-Mr. Gelber for Nipissing (Mr. Legault) is a valued member and we welcome him as well to this historic House.
In a searching discussion of the problems of youth, Professor Erikson writes:
Fidelity could not mature earlier in life, and must not in the crises of youth, fail its time of ascendance if human adaptation is to remain intact.. .Here again diversity and fidelity are polarized.. .fidelity without a sense of diversity can become an obsession and a bore.. .diversity without a sense of fidelity..."
-can become empty. The role of youth is crucial in our society and this Government sets an important horizon in organizing a Company of Young Canadians. The Professor of Human Development at Harvard continues:
In youth, then, the life history intersects with history: here individuals are confirmed in their identities, societies regenerated in their life style.
E. E. Cohen, executive secretary, National Child Labour Committee, is concerned about "early physical maturation combined with delayed social responsibility". This program of the Government of Canada to provide a wider context of service meets in some measure what has been called the moratorium of responsibility. Some feel that youth is too preoccupied with solving personal problems and problems of adjustment. Professor Erikson writes:
-but in youth the tables of childhood dependence begin slowly to turn: no longer is it merely for the old to teach the young the meaning of life, whether individual or collective. It is the young who, by their responses and actions, tell the old whether life as represented by the old and as presented to the young has meaning; and it is the young who carry in them the power to confirm those who confirm them and, joining the issues, to renew and to regenerate, or to reform and to rebel.
This historic role meets new challenges in the nuclear age.
The youth of Canada is prepared to meet the challenge which the Company of Young Canadians offers. We do not accept the tragic ethic expressed in the story from Greek myths told by the ancient historian Herodotus about two youths, Kleobis and Biton, of remarkable strength, who were victorious in many gymnastic games and drew the chariot of their mother, Hera, a priestess, a great distance to the sanctuary of Argos. She prayed to the gods to reward her sons and as their greatest gift, allowed the two brothers to die in their sleep in the fulness of their youth. Our ideal is the fulness of life, and in providing added avenues for social responsibility for the youth of Canada the Company of Young Canadians can play a historic role.

Dr. Harold Taylor, a well known Canadian points out:
We do find changes taking place in the attitudes of students towards themselves and towards their society. These changes occur when two major factors are present. The first is the presence of idealistic, sensitive teachers who care about their students and who develop ways of helping them to find the guidance they need. The second is a community life in which the students are called upon to concern themselves with their relationships to each other and to their world, not merely on the extroverted basis provided by sports and social engagements, but by the structure of the community itself.
The effort of Canadians in two world wars is a most remarkable one. About a million Canadians volunteered for service overseas 1939-45 and the honour role contains 41,992 who paid the supreme sacrifice in corners of foreign fields that will always remain part of our Canadian heritage. Our country has had this great tradition of voluntary service both in peace and war. The names of many battles are hallowed in the history of our country where with skill and bravery Canadians fought for a common cause. Some volunteered again in the Pacific area and during the United Nations collective security action in Korea Canadian volunteers carried the colours of famous Canadian regiments. We can paraphase the famous English poet, A. E. Housman who wrote: "It dawns in Asia. Tombstones show"-and Canadian names are read.
I know the House would want to hear again this excerpt from the citation on the awarding of the Victoria Cross to Captain (acting Major) Paul Triquet, Royal 22nd Regiment. Upon instructing soldiers in security I always read the entire citation and I am pleased to recall it today.
Against bitter and determined defence and under heavy fire, Captain Triquet and his company in close co-operation with the tanks, forced their way on until a position was reached on the outskirts of Casa Berardi. By this time the strength of the company was reduced to two sergeants and 15 men. In expectation of a counterattack, Captain Triquet at once set about organizing his handful of men into a defensive perimeter around the remaining tanks and passed the mot d'ordre "Ils ne passe-ront pas". A German counterattack supported by tanks developed almost immediately. Captain Triquet, ignoring the heavy fire, was everywhere encouraging his men and directing the defence, and by using whatever weapons were to hand personally accounted for several of the enemy. This and subsequent attacks were beaten off with heavy losses and Captain Triquet and his small force held out against overwhelming odds until the remainder of the battalion took Casa Berardi and relieved them the next day.
April 13, 1965

Now, Mr. Speaker, we have been told that the idea of a Company of Young Canadians has been borrowed. Ideas are always borrowed. They are borrowed, reinterpreted and rearranged. We have been told that many ideas in the Speech from the Throne have been borrowed, and of course they have. They have been matured and mellowed by experience and they will be applied to the problems of Canada. That is the test of any government, to make a political reality out of a good idea. The idea of a program of service is something that springs from deep wells within Canadian life.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I would like to say a word about a very successful project, CUSO-the Canadian University Service Overseas. CUSO is organized on the basis of a partnership between the CUSO organization and the university that is recruiting personnel, because this is a student organization. CUSO selects, trains and transports the students. The host country provides them with local salary, room and board and an appropriate allowance. A Ghanaian official said this:
I am extremely suspicious of the "dedicated person" who wishes to help but has no specific skill. Don't send underdeveloped people to underdeveloped countries.
Its personnel must be screened, carefully selected and trained. Training programs for them before they go abroad have been conducted at the University of British Columbia, McGill University, the University of Montreal and the University of Toronto. Here is what was said by an educator from Tibet about one CUSO worker:
Due to her intense devotion to work and her medical knowledge we have been able to bring a tremendous improvement in the school. This school was primarily established for children who are so weak that they need particular care. So the task here is demanding. She has been wonderful with the children and they have taken a great liking to her.
In addition to intellectual ability, candidates must possess emotional maturity, resourcefulness and must be able to adapt themselves to the unfamiliar. They must be willing to regard their overseas assignment as an opportunity for learning through service, and they must have the capacity to conduct themselves at all times with humility and understanding. This is not only a process for serving others; it is a process for serving ourselves, for learning. Here is a story from Ghana. Two CUSO students were married in Ghana, and here is a letter which one of them wrote:
I'm afraid the only excuse I can offer for this late report is my marriage to fellow CUSO volun-
The Address-Mr. Gelber teer, John Baigent, and perhaps you'll see from my description just how hectic things have been. We were delighted when Terry Bacon, Third Secretary of the Canadian High Commission, responded by offering to give the reception as his gift.
One thing led to another. Since the wedding reception was out of our hands, we could then afford invitations and we had great fun trying to convince the African printer that we did not want elaborate cards covered with silver bells and cupids. We ended up with a design somewhere between African and Canadian tastes and had a marvellous time sending off 250 invitations-although we knew that 200 of the invited people would be too far away to come. It made us feel a little bit closer to the folks back home anyway.
No wedding is complete without a cake and once again we had fun with the African baker, convincing him that we were people of very simple tastes and didn't really want bells, cupids, hearts, etc., adorning our cake. The Africans love bright colours, gaudy decorations, etc., and their tradesmen reflect the philosophy that if a little bit is good, then lots is better I But we won-simplicity prevailed.
Mr. Speaker, under the Canadian University Service Overseas, Canada has sent a group of students to a wide number of countries around the world. The Globe and Mail reports some of them wrote back:
"No matter how much you prepare, you're rocked when you arrive," says Don Millar of Toronto, a 22-year-old history graduate teaching English in Dhampur, Uttar Pradesh.
"The heat and the faces just crowd in upon you", says Martha Nixon, 21, of Montreal, McGill graduate in psychology and anthropology, who is teaching at Balarampur, West Bengal.
"But the initial impression that our living conditions here were primitive and dirty has already worn off," adds Montrealer Stephen Jasper, 22, another McGill graduate, who is teaching English at Jamal Mohamed college in Tiruchirapalli, Madras State.
"India can be daunting-You're such a drop in a huge bucket, as one student put it-but the 10 young men and nine young women display no lack of enthusiasm, only a measure of humility about how much enthusiasm can accomplish.
"My greatest fear is that I somehow may not fit into the educational system, won't be able to communicate," says Terry McElroy, 22, of Ottawa, a Queen's University graduate teaching English at Padhampali High School in Orissa province."
There are other programs of service for students. Here is one described in the Ottawa
Citizen:
A group of 180 Canadian university students, 54 of them from Ottawa, will spend part of their summer holiday in the Mexican hinterland trying to improve the lot of the less fortunate. What makes this project a particular challenge is that they have to raise funds to pay the costs of transportation and the bare essentials of living.
Here is another program at present being carried on in Canada by The International
COMMONS DEBATES	April 13, 1965
The Address-Mr. Gelber
Grenfell Association. This information was supplied to me by the hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. O'Keefe):
These.. .are.. .young men and women who have recently finished what would be equivalent to our high school, and are just prior to entering university. These students come on the coast for various lengths of time, as orderlies, voluntary workers of one type or another. We have medical students who come on a rotational basis the year around, with the largest number coming during the summer months. These students come from various universities in Canada, the United States and England. During the summer months, we have short term volunteer workers from universities of Canada and the U.S.A., mainly, who do volunteer work in our dormitories, hospitals, and community work in various areas.
Then I have information here about Operation Beaver, 1965, a Canadian Ecumenical Council project. There is a whole series of projects listed here by the Student Christian Movement. Here is another group of projects listed by the Vocational Register, Student Christian Movement of Canada. There is a wide variety of voluntary programs, not only for students but at all levels in Canada. The voluntary tradition is an important tradition in Canada, and I believe that a proper challenge to the youth of Canada-not only to the students but to all the youth of Canada- will meet with a most happy response. The British, the French, the Dutch, the Scandinavians, the Australians all have programs of assistance abroad. I have information here about a great number of these. I would like to say just a word about the largest of these, and that is the United States Peace Corps. The then Senator Hubert Humphrey, now Vice President of the United States, in introducing the Peace Corps legislation into the Senate on June 1, 1961, said this:
The Peace Corps which has been set up under Executive order will cost less than the cost of firing one Atlas missile, even one that does not work. The anticipated first year's budget for the Peace Corps will cost one tenth of 1 per cent of what it will take to put a man on the moon.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
For the Peace Corps program the host country credits the Corps with a significant role in its development. Every nation in which the Peace Corps is serving is asking for more volunteers. Additional countries are also asking for Peace Corps participation in upbuilding.
I think it is symptomatic that the Ramon Magsaysay Philippines award which has been considered as one of Asia's prime awards was given to a Peace Corps Director, Sergeant Shriver, on behalf of the Volunteers, who had

served in 11 Asian countries by 1962. It was the first time this award has been given to a non-Asian.
There are many types of individuals that the United States Peace Corps invites for participation. It wants physicians, both general practitioners and specialists, registered nurses, licensed practical nurses, health directors, medical technicians, physical technicians, hospital administrators and many others.
There is also a great deal of work for manual labourers in the Peace Corps. Jim McKay volunteered to serve in the Peace Corps and is now working in Lahore, Pakistan, helping to build a hospital. The average bricklayer there lays 225 bricks per day, whereas Jim's average is 750, and his skill is being used to help his Pakistani co-workers improve their own production.
There are important tasks at home which a Canadian corps of service could perform. Certainly the more obvious might be those relating to our Indian and Eskimo populations. There are all types of Group Workers needed in the most advanced and mature urban societies, as well as in the less advantageous urban areas.
We know of the work that is being done through ARDA. There is a demand for young Canadians to serve and assist in the type of work that ARDA is doing. They can do much to help with these important tasks. The frontiers of this country are great and the imagination and challenges which this Government can offer to the youth of Canada I am sure will meet with hearty response.
We hear a great deal about youth, and I was very interested when I found a quotation from Socrates who lived about 2,400 years ago. Socrates said:
Our youth now loves luxury. They have bad manners and contempt for authority. They show disrespect for their elders and love idle chatter in place of exercise. Children are now tyrants-not the servants of the household. They no longer rise when elders enter the room. They contradict their parents, chatter before company, gobble up their food and tyrannize their teachers.
I believe that both at home and abroad there are great tasks, great challenges and great opportunities for the youth of Canada, which is responding and will continue to respond. I think the Government is to be congratulated for bringing before this Parliament the idea of a Company of Young Canadians to serve both at home and abroad -to give service to others and to serve themselves.
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Pascoe
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from Sir Rabindranath Tagore, the Indian poet and philosopher, who once said:
Man goes into the noisy crowd to drown the clamour of his own silence.
Canadian youth will go forward into the crowd to find itself and its fulfilment.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to join with others in congratulating the Mover and Seconder of the Speech from the Throne. Their efforts are all the more commendable because of the vague generalities contained in the Speech. It contains plenty of fancy frosting on the cake, but not much cake to bite into. It contains promises but lacks detail.
I agree with many views expressed by editorial writers and T.V. commentators, that this is a pre-election speech which is not actually intended for full implementation during this session of Parliament. It was meant more for possible vote catching. The date of the coming election is not revealed in the Speech, but the intent is certainly there.
Many speakers have dealt at some length with what the Speech contains, and more particularly with what it does not contain. I should like to refer to three or four items which have not been covered during this debate. One item in the Throne Speech deals with what is described as "comprehensive legislation to reform public regulation of the railways". This really should read "reform of last session's legislation, Bill C-120". This is just another example of the Government being forced to revise ill-considered legislation hastily produced.
We have held some worth-while meetings of the Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines and I am sure the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has had certain deficiencies of Bill C-120 forcibly drawn to his attention. I should now like to draw his attention to the Sixth National Farm and Business Forum, held in Winnipeg recently under the sponsorship of the Agricultural Bureau of the Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce.
A large number of individuals were in attendance at this conference, all of whom expressed opinions. While I do not intend to outline every opinion expressed, I should like to refer to one or two and place them on record, so that they will come to the attention of the Minister of Transport.
The first statement to which I wish to refer was made by Mr. A. V. Mauro, Q.C., Chairman of the Manitoba Transport Commission. He said that-
-national policy of rail rationalization was necessary and the primary objective of this should be to enhance the political and economic welfare of the Canadian people.
He then went on to say that-
-if any rationalization program is proposed for railway systems in the prairie provinces it should be worked out on a basis much wider than merely the solely related formula of railway submission.
Mr. Mauro then stated that-
-any appointed authority should consider an over-all pattern rather than a simple point to point approach undertaken by rail companies.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
Here is another statement, this time by Hon. George Taylor, Minister of Highways for Alberta. He stated five points which I should like to put on the record.
1.	That a rationalization authority should be established with full responsibility to deal with rail line abandonment and with power to order the interchange of lines, the seasonal use of lines and the exchange of running rights between two or more railways. It should also have power to deal with costs and revenues before and after and would not be required to deal only with costs and revenues at the time of application.
2.	That all authority dealing with the abandonment of rail lines presently in the hands of the Board of Transport Commissioners, be transferred to the rationalization authority.
3.	That the rationalization authority be given full power to order the Board of Transport to carry out studies affecting the railways and the results of such studies should be transmitted to the authority without recommendation for a final decision.
4.	That the rationalization authority be given full power to deal with governments at all levels, the railways, businesses and all others in the area and region that will be affected by the abandonment of a branch line.
5.	The rationalization authority should be required to give extra weight to any item adversely affecting the favourable position of Canadian grain in world markets.
I want to emphasize that last point because I come from a grain producing area where the people are very much interested in the whole railway problem and especially in the problem of rail line abandonment. Mr. E. A. Boden, vice president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, also spoke and he said:
Abandonment of branch lines on the scale sought by the railways will cause major disruption of the grain industry.. . He said it would mean the removal of 3,453 miles of tracks and 923 country elevators which would cost approximately $60 million to replace.
Again I am emphasizing this because of my interest in the grain producing area from which I come. Mr. Boden continued:
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Pascoe
A federal authority concerned with branch line abandonment should have the power to act rather than to just recommend changes.
With respect to the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and other organizations he said:
They hold the view that whatever body is given the responsibility for deciding the fate of rail lines, should have the authority and the ability to examine the broad picture, to look at areas rather than single lines.
An article in the Western Producer summed up the conference and I should like to put part of it on the record:
It was significant that much of the time during the sessions was taken up with wide-ranging discussion of the shortcomings of the now defunct Bill C-120.
I think we can all agree with that because the Government has withdrawn that Bill. Then there is a reference to Mr. Boden to whom I have already referred:
Mr. E. A. Boden, Saskatchewan Wheat Pool second vice president, following a graphic description of the final results of the closure of all branch lines now proposed by the railway companies for abandonment, gave a number of interesting examples of possible rationalization. These included situations in which there could be line sharing and interchange of running rights, the bridging of existing gaps so that routes of access to main lines could be shortened, and other devices which appear perfectly feasible and desirable. It was interesting to note that no railway representative at the meeting offered critcism of Mr. Boden's proposals.
There is one other aspect of the railway problem to which I wish to refer briefly. It concerns reports of the curtailment of passenger services, particularly by the Canadian Pacific Railway. In this connection I wish to put on the record a resolution passed at the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan Urban Municipalities Association in Regina on April 2 last. It reads as follows:
Whereas the C.P.R. has been granted land, mineral and tax concessions in the early days of its operation, and
Whereas an expanding population and economy requires a comprehensive transportation system for such growth, and
Whereas the C.P.R. has shown a disregard for the public interest and intends to discontinue passenger rail service even though the C.N.R. has increased passenger rail service profit by some 19 per cent,
Be it resolved that this assembly go on record as insisting upon the consideration of public interest before any further discontinuance of C.P.R. passenger train service is allowed, and
Be it further resolved that no additional curtailment of existing passenger service be allowed by the Board of Transport until a full inquiry is held by the Federal Government to determine whether the public is able to obtain space on present facilities.

Many in my riding are not convinced that the C.P.R. is making every possible effort to improve passenger traffic and they think the company should make this extra effort. Apparently Canadian National Railways has met with considerable success in its campaign to interest more people in travelling by rail. I would refer to the annual report of the C.N.R. just received where on page 9 there is this notation in regard to passenger services:
Sales. The number of passengers carried by C.N. increased in 1964 by 14.0 per cent over 1963 and passenger service revenues were 16.7 per cent higher. The red, white and blue fare plan, to which is credited much of the increase in passenger sales, was extended throughout the system during 1964 and this and other passenger sales projects were intensively advertised and promoted in various ways.
I read this as a challenge to the C.P.R. also to go out after passenger traffic, and I am quite sure they would be able to get it. I know we are trying to finish tonight, Mr. Speaker, and I do not want to take too much time but there is one more point to which I should like to refer because I am quite concerned about this matter. As I said before, I come from a wheat producing area. Early in the Speech from the Throne there appears this reference:
My Government is resolved that Canada shall make the fullest contribution it can to the lessening of international tensions, including the provision of practical assistance to developing countries.
I suggest that one way to extend practical assistance to developing countries is to provide greater help with regard to their food problems. I know that this Government and the previous Government have participated in the world food program under F.A.O. I believe we are the third largest contributor to this program under which distributions of skim milk, cheese, butter oil, dried fish, flour and oats have been made to 15 countries mostly in Asia and Africa. This particular food aid project was started in January, 1963 by the Diefenbaker Government. It seems to me that Canada could do much more to meet the food needs of underdeveloped countries. I am thinking particularly of our great stocks of wheat that are again beginning to pile up, despite the brave words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp). There are problems in regard to our commercial wheat markets, but a more extensive food aid program of wheat and wheat flour should not interfere with our regular markets. It would certainly help the developing countries. Previous gifts of
April 13, 1965

wheat and wheat flour brought the first taste of bread to millions who now welcome bread as a staple diet. Canada should do more to satisfy this demand.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, this is a good time to take issue, as I have done in this House on previous occasions, with those who advocate diets that do not include bread. Some of these advocates of no-bread meals are in this Parliament. I have a copy of such a diet here and the chart says that you must not eat bread or anything containing starch or flour. This is a diet to which I take very strong exception, Mr. Speaker. I cannot put it in better words than I find in this particular farm journal, and I quote:
Diet fads may easily do harm which can never be erased, as can posture fads, high heel fads, and any number of others. In food, fads have again and again thrown nutrition out of balance in a shocking proportion of the population. Bread and potatoes, the most common starch suppliers, have been repeatedly cast in the villain's role....
None of these foods is either villain or hero on its own. In a balanced diet each can and does play an excellent part. It is the silliness of fadism which gets them all out of proportion in human eating habits.
I have a news item here, Mr. Speaker, which may explain the no-bread diet of some of our friends. The article is headed "Soft Life Reduces Wheat Consumption". I quote:
A higher income is associated with the "soft life" and a minimum of physical exercise-desk work, driving instead of walking to the neighbourhood store, and hiring someone to do the odd jobs around the house. As a result, the need for high-caloric foods is reduced.
A bigger pay cheque also allows a family to indulge to a greater degree in the more expensive food items, thus creating a larger demand for meats and fruits at the expense of low priced items such as bread.
I am trying, as I said, to contradict this no-bread diet, and I think in the interests of good health I should. I should like to refer briefly to the suggestions of the nutrition division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Here, I have "Canada's Food Guide," indicating the foods to eat every day, and bread and cereals are certainly very much played up. Then, there is another copy of "Canada's Food Guide", and it advocates bread and cereals very day for good health. This pamphlet is from the Health League of Canada and is headed "Every Week is Health Week." I have quoted this before and it advocates at least four slices of bread a day.
These are just a few items relating to the health qualities of bread, Mr. Speaker. I should like to refer briefly to an article con-
The Address-Mr. Pascoe cerning foods and nutrition in Japan and India. I quote:
Long ago Japan realized the nutritional dangers of using rice to the exclusion of other foods and the advantage of using wheat and other cereal products as well as rice in their diet.
Then, with regard to India, the article says:
Although India is considered to be a rice eating country, half the population look on wheat as part of their staple diet.
I should like to quote an article from "Grain Market Features":
Speaking in London recently, Sir Charles Dodds, one of the world's acknowledged leaders in the field of nutrition referred to...the food value of cereals and the fact that cereals would go farther and were capable of contributing more to the maintenance of human life, more economically, than any other food product...
He added that experience over the' centuries had shown that life could be maintained adequately on bread alone, and if this was supplemented by vegetables and possibly small quantities of dairy products a high standard of nutrition could be maintained.
In concluding my argument with regard to bread I should like to quote this article from the Family Herald:
Canadian consumption of bread has tended to fall on a per capita basis as our standard of living has risen. Yet it would be a sorry day if flour ever became too much taken for granted by Canadians. With our enormous wheatlands, we are the custodians of perhaps the most important food crop the white man has ever known.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I am from a bread eating area of Canada, the Prairies. My diet consists of at least four slices of bread daily. I do not believe I am too much overweight, and I am in good health. The young women of the Prairies eat bread and they are slim and attractive. They raise fine families of healthy bread-eaters. I am sure their measurements would compare with those who are skimping on bread. I had some exhibits in the gallery a short time ago, but unfortunately they have gone.
I have one more small item to which 1 should like to refer with regard to the Speech from the Throne. Actually, reference was made to it by the hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin! yesterday. He referred to the big problem in that area of the very large stocks of damp wheat. I should like to draw to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), who is in charge of the Board of Grain Commissioners, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), who is in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, the fact that in my city of Moose Jaw there is a large Canadian Government elevator equipped with the finest
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Fisher and most modern facilities for drying grain. It is not being used at this moment. I suggest to these Ministers that they look into the situation carefully. I think at very little expense they could move that wheat to this elevator at Moose Jaw, dry it and sell it at a much better price, a price which would cover the cost of drying.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is a
pleasure, Mr. Acting Speaker (Mr. Tardif) to see you in the Chair. I know your reputation for never missing votes, and it is nice to see that has been recognized by giving you this higher responsibility. In connection with votes, I want to say that of all the votes that have taken place here in the last few years, the one I regret most missing was the one last Friday on the main motion of nonconfidence. I regret missing it because I believe completely in the indictment that condemned this Government particularly for carelessness, indifference and neglect of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in refusing to take action to eradicate wrongdoing in high and low places under Federal responsibility, and restore public confidence in the honesty and integrity of the Government.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
The question that still remains in my mind, despite the vote I was not here to take part in, really centres on the fact that I cannot believe the story that we have had in connection with a number of items, particularly in relation to the Prime Minister's conduct and the conduct of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) in the whole matter relating to the Rivard inquiry.
One of the things that most concerns me is the uneven, one might almost call it the random justice which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) seems to be so proud of. In his speech during this debate he thundered out how quickly he acted in connection with his Parliamentary Secretary. He acted very quickly with his Parliamentary Secretary, yet nothing has been proven against his Parliamentary Secretary. He acted very quickly with the Minister without Portfolio, and nothing has been yet proven against the Minister without Portfolio. He gave us no explanation of his actions in either case, other than it is quite obvious he thinks he has proven his ability to react in such a situation by the abrupt dismissal he has given those two men.
I have no brief for them, but I am very much bothered by the fact that the Prime Minister will make a virtue out of a curt dismissal like that of two of his advisers and yet, at the same time, have a completely different attitude to other people and other Ministers, for example the Minister of Justice, for example the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the matter of the Onofrio Mainaudo case, for example the gentlemen with their furniture. All that seems to be fine.
We have the situation that the hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) referred to, that the postal employees in this country are up in arms and enraged because they feel they have been slurred by the minister they have been given as a result of the minor shake-up coming out of these scandals. I was interested this afternoon in hearing one of the Government supporters giving the hon. Member for Yukon the devil for his tactics in raising these things, especially the serious question that brought about the Dorion Inquiry.
What do my friends on the Government side think the situation would have been if the Government had been in a comfortable majority? Do you think we would have had the terms of the Dorion Inquiry altered? Do you think we would not have been shut off completely? We certainly would. It is only as the result of vigilance-and I give a great deal of credit to the hon. Member for Yukon [DOT]-that we can begin to probe what I think is the most dangerous aspect of this Government, and that is its wishy-washy attitude towards its own integrity.
There is the difference between integrity and performance, or inept performance, and a lot of the ineptitude, the boneheaded plays of the Government do not have any relationship to the whole question I am talking about. They just reflect the general weakness of the Ministry and the Cabinet. I do not know whether we should feel sorry or sympathetic for some of the supporters of the Government, who have to sit behind it and put up with the performance of this Ministry.
One of the points I wanted to make in connection with this whole question of integrity and morality is to say how absurd I think it is that the Minister of Justice has made the kind of defence that he has. I wanted to put on the record-and of course this is in translation-what I consider his corny melodramatic, indefensible kind of reaction to his own stupidity and ineptitude in the performance of his chores. He gave a speech on Friday and this is what he said:
[Mr. Pascoe.l

Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks I wish to challenge the remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who, during the first ten minutes of his speech, endeavoured to reactivate and rehash all the supposed scandals which were blamed on the present administration. I think this is merely a storm in a teapot. I will soon start reading the book entitled "Douglas in Saskatchewan." I am told that it is better than "The Renegade in Power" written by Paul Newman. I am anxious to read it because it seems to be very interesting. I cannot pursue the same line as the hon. member for Port Arthur who tried to demolish the Speech from the Throne. Knowing him as we do, we could hardly expect him to congratulate the present government.
May I now add my congratulations to those addressed by the previous speakers to the mover (Mr. Cashin) and the seconder (Mr. Chretien) of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne for the brilliant and eloquent way they discharged their functions.
We already knew that they were gifted; we were convinced that they would do their duty honourably. Their constituents must be proud to have elected men of that caliber to represent them in the house.
Most newspapers, Mr. Speaker, are practically unanimous in stating in big type that this speech from the throne is one of the most comprehensive ever presented by a government. It is true that it deals with all sectors of national activity.
Special mention is made in this speech of international and domestic matters, in the economic and industrial as well as social fields. Every field is mentioned, which prompt certain members of the opposition to suggest it is an electoral manifesto. Whether it is or not, one fact remains: the government
The Address-Mr. Loiselle is ready and willing, after due consideration, to submit to this house the legislation required to improve living conditions in all fields. It is a frontal attack on all problems facing the Canadian citizens and what pleases me most, it is a war on poverty that the government is determined to launch. On the whole, about 30 different items are put forward in this speech.
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to belong to a team which gives the people of Canada a government which is concerned with the welfare of its citizens, which has the courage to face all the problems which Canadians, young and old, have to face.
In the course of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I intend to comment on only two or three of the main items in this impressive speech.
One of the proposed measures deals with the need to reform the procedure of the House of Commons so that the legislative work can be done more quickly. We all know in what atmosphere this house has worked over the last 12 months and, personally, I am not proud of it.
In spite of the foul punches it got and the obstruction and delaying tactics it had to put up with during the last session of parliament, the government did more for the advancement of Canada than any of its predecessors did for a good many years.
Very often during the last session, long and useless speeches were made for the deliberate purpose of impeding the proper functioning of this house. For the past several months, in talks on the radio during the program "Report from parliament hill", I have advocated a change in our rules which is called for now more than ever. One thing which proves it clearly is that everyone has heard certain members of the opposition state, when they were asked about their impressions on the speech from the throne, that parliament now has worked for two years to come.
The government has certainly work for two years to come if things go the way they did during last session. I would not perhaps say two years but more; this is why we should amend our rules.
A maximum of eight days is now provided for the throne speech debate and a maximum of six days for the budget debate. Why could the same time limit not be set for the discussion of other government legislation? I am in favour of freedom of speech, but freedom of speech of certain persons or groups must not interfere with the freedom of action of the government.
April 13. 1965

The Address-Mr. Loiselle
A government is elected with the assent and consent of the people. The people who elect all members of the house have no use for dull speeches which do nothing to improve legislation. What Canadians want is serious work, painstaking so that all may benefit by the legislation which the members of the house are called upon to vote. If the present government proposes legislation that is not in the interests of the population, it will be up to the people, at the next election, to express their views on the laws already voted and on the measures the government will have brought before the house. In other words, I eagerly hope, Mr. Speaker, that, upon our return from the Easter recess, the question of procedural changes will be brought before the house.
One of the major concerns of the Prime Minister and the members of his party, is national unity. All the actions of the government during the last two years prove it. In the speech from the throne we find that same interest for unity which, in spite of the opposition of some people, and some groups, will shine brightly and forever.
As soon as this government was elected to office, after the election of April 1963, there was a sigh of relief in anticipation of the future, of happier days compared to those we had lived through in the recent past.
In fact, everyone can notice-even those who do not support the government, those who, for the last two years, have been criticizing, rightly or wrongly, any legislation proposed by the government-an expansion of trade, an increase in salaries, an increase in our exports, which is but the beginning. It is said that figures do not lie; let those who are prompted to criticize look at those figures. They will see for themselves a substantial increase in all areas.
Mr. Speaker, another matter which is of great concern to me is unemployment. Although unemployment is at its lowest level for years, the government does not think that the problem is solved by any means. We know that the percentage is still too high. That is why the government is taking steps to remedy the situation; it shows its willingness to take action in order to reduce the number of unemployed. Unemployment is now at its lowest level since 1957.
In the field of industry, there has been new expansion for the last two years. The forecasts are to the effect that 1965 will be one of the better years yet.

[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
As far as old age security is concerned, the situation has improved. I admit that it could be better than it is now, but in any field progress must be gradual. "In order to give with one hand, one must have something in the other".
Even if in the last two years of the administration of the business of the country, progress and a better social security have been achieved, even if all spheres of our Canadian society have known, for the last two years, a better lot, this government, aware of its responsibilities, admits in its speech from the throne that there is much to do. Here I would like to quote a paragraph to that effect:
Our country Is achieving a higher rate of economic growth. Trade is expanding. With growing industrialization, Canadians are enjoying rapidly increasing employment opportunities; incomes and living standards are rising: the number of people out of work has been reduced to lower levels than for many years.
All the great potentialities of our economy are not, however, being realized. The talents of some of our people are wasted because of poverty, illness, inadequate education and training, inequality in opportunities for work. To combat these problems, to improve the opportunities of people who are now at a disadvantage, is to put new power into economic expansion and to enhance the unity of our country.
Some have criticized those who express an awareness for those problems still facing our country, but I do not see anything wrong with the admission that, despite our many achievements, there is still much to do in order to provide better living conditions for one and all and not only for a part of our society. It is a recognized fact that a part of the population has much difficulty in finding work necessary to meet their needs, due to automation and their lack of training to adapt to our modern industries.
Being the representative of a working class district, one of the oldest wards of Montreal, I am aware of the difficulty workers experience in finding employment. I welcome the proposals announced in the speech from the throne to correct this situation. I hope that all my hon. friends, being aware of the seriousness of this problem, will support this legislation which will tend to the welfare of the working class.
The worst tragedy for the head of a family is to lose his job or to be unemployed; this prevents him from providing for the needs of his family and he suffers even more when he is forced to refuse to his children certain amenities which their friends have. Knowing the problem and its effects on society, I wel-
April 13. 1965

come the action of the government which is determined to tackle this matter. It is a fact that, rightly or wrongly, too many people do not realize why they are unemployed. They expect that the higher level of government will provide them with the job they want. There must be co-ordination between the municipal, provincial and federal administrations and also suggestions of reforms by large and small businesses to correct the social evil of unemployment.
These last few years, the winter works subsidized by the federal government have contributed to reduce the number of jobless in winter. It is the duty of every administration, whatever its level, to provide for the future of our workers. At present, unemployment strikes those who have not enough education or no trade, the so-called labourers.
The city of Montreal is going through a period of fantastic development in the field of building, road and subway construction and the preparations for the 1967 world fair. In spite of all that activity, the unemployed who do not have the necessary training to adapt themselves to modern equipment cannot find work to provide for their needs, for their own welfare and that of their families. Consequently, I am happy to foresee better times for all those who will benefit from the action the government intends to take in that respect.
In another field, Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne states that the government will give special consideration to the problem of urban renewal in several communities.
I have always been concerned with that and, during the very first session I had the pleasure and the honour of representing my constituents here, I considered it my duty to call it to the attention of the government then in power. On several instances, both here and at the municipal council of the city of Montreal, I mentioned that question which is of vital importance for the people of my riding. As a Montreal alderman, I sat on the committee which prepared and realized the only low rental housing project in the province of Quebec and which was carried out in Montreal under the name of "Habitations Jeanne-Mance".
On many occasions, I stated publicly my regret that no other such project has been executed since. All those who are familiar with Montreal know that the administration must face that problem. Renewal projects should be carried out in several parts of the city, and I could add especially in my riding. As I said previously, the problem of urban re-
The Address-Mr. Loiselle newal in Montreal is of such scope that to make a complete job of it, that is to expropriate, demolish and rebuild, it must be tackled on a 20 to 40 year basis, at great expense to the city.
I now raise the problem of urban renewal in Montreal, knowing that the minister responsible for C.M.H.C. is fully aware of it. He even held discussions with the Quebec minister of municipal affairs and with the municipal authorities on the subject. The town planning division of the city of Montreal, composed of competent men, has been making thorough studies for more than a year to promote the type of renewal most appropriate to the present needs of Montreal.
This renewal program now proposed by the city council has been known for some time, but it has some special characteristics, in that it does not comply with all the beneficial provisions of the C.M.H.C. legislation. Therefore, I intend to submit this problem to the House in order to suggest amendments to that legislation so that this program might be carried out.
The renewal program suggested now by the administration is brand new and it is, I think, the only one to have ever been proposed by the municipal government of any city in North America. What allows me to bring this problem to the attention of the house is the fact that the area now designated for renewal is located in the municipal district I represent at City Hall; besides, the major part of that area lies in my federal riding and that of my colleague from St. Henry (Mr. Lessard). This pilot area covers 265 acres; it has been called "Petite Bourgogne". After all the necessary inquiries and studies required under the C.M.H.C. legislation, it has now been recognized as a renewal area by that corporation and by the Quebec minister of municipal affairs.
It is of the utmost importance that some amendments be made to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act to encourage the renewal which is so badly needed in Montreal and to ensure at the same time the welfare of all those families who live in the said district. An agreement has already been reached by the corporation's office and the municipal administration, and the city has already taken advantage of the act to set up in that area two new recreation parks.
Unfortunately, with the passing of time and due to circumstances, that 265-acre residential section had only one very small park
