For instance, it has been found after a survey had been made in the area chosen, that 84 buildings had been built prior to 1874. The whole range follows: Between 1875 and 1884, 347 buildings; between 1885 and 1894, 430; and among the most recent constructions, 16 were erected between 1935 and 1944; 35, between 1945 and 1954; and 20, between 1955 and 1964.
Out of a total of 1,495 buildings, in this area, 1,281 had been erected prior to 1914. Needless to say that these buildings no longer meet today's requirements. This proves immediately the urgent need to renew this area and, also, an urgent need for provincial and federal assistance.
Even with such assistance from higher level governments, the city is assuming a heavy burden for the municipal budget. The magnitude of the additional charges imposed on the Montreal taxpayers are an added responsibility.
The alarming aspect of the situation, which creates an urgent necessity, is the fact that for

the last 20 years, the resident population of that district has been decreasing from year to year. The area to be renovated is only a few steps from down town and it will become one of the best residential sites for those who want to take up residence there. I am therefore pleased to note in the speech from the throne that special attention will be paid to the renewal of the blighted and congested areas, which will promote the welfare of the residents.
Finally, the object of urban renewal in that 265-acre area can be carried out in seven stages:	1. Redevelopment of some small
islands; 2. Demolition and reconstruction of some buildings on various small islands; 3. Restoration of houses which may be economically repaired; 4. Application of measures for the preservation of buildings in good condition; 5. Low rent housing; 6. Necessary adjustments to the infrastructure of the area; 7. Adequate collective equipment.
All this cannot be paid for by the taxpayers of beautiful Montreal without federal and provincial government assistance.
Needless to continue to prove that such renewal is necessary; it is a moral obligation and, in this connection, I should like to make the following suggestions to the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, so that this renewal be carried out expeditiously without neglecting renewal of other areas where it is equally warranted.
It would be advisable, in the future, in order to speed consideration of each new area so that it may be approved by both the department of municipal affairs of Quebec and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, that the Montreal district office, responsible to the corporation, be empowered to approve a definite area, after having summarily examined the site, without waiting, as the act requires today, for every examination reports to be submitted. This would help speed up renewal of future areas. Furthermore, the act should be amended to favour such renewal: 1. By accepting the principle of grants for renewal purposes; 2. -grants for demolition and rebuilding; 3.-grants for rents.
In the latter case, it is a monthly grant intended to make up for the rent, the value of which would be determined by the difference between the rental value roll of the city of Montreal and the rent an individual may pay according to his income.
When considering the high cost of urban renewal, we should also take into account that price is no object when the welfare of
April 13, 1965	COMMONS
almost half the population, the normal development of family life and liberty of community life are involved.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, may I touch lightly on the project for a harbour station in the city of Montreal.
When the main estimates were tabled recently by the Minister of Finance, an amount of $1 million was provided for the construction of a harbour station in Montreal. This need has existed for several years. At the present time, passengers have to embark and disembark by going through sheds that are being used as warehouses. Such a thing is inconceivable, especially when it happens in this country's metropolis. The building of a harbour station in Montreal is urgent; we have heard about it for years and now we have almost reached the goal.
I should like, at this stage, to emphasize certain facts which would favour the building of this harbour station at the lower end or in the vicinity of McGill street. Other places have often been mentioned, but I do not think there would be a more appropriate place than the southwestern part of Montreal, namely on the western side of the harbour; it would be the ideal place, a short distance from the centre of the city, from hotels, department stores, railway stations, the entrance to the world fair or from the approach to the bridges giving access to all the main highways in the province.
I have in the past made representations to the proper authorities, and I wish to state that I hope to see that harbour station erected in the southwestern area of the city of Montreal which is in every way an ideal location.
I trust that in the very near future the Government, through the Department of Transport, will announce the site selected for the construction of that station.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I hope that all the members of the house, as representatives of the people, will promote their welfare by supporting all the measures proposed in the throne speech, in order that all Canadian citizens may be happy and proud to live in that beautiful and great country of ours.

speechtext:
As we have not reached unanimity, I will make a few remarks on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
As usual, I associate myself with those who preceded me in congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) for the way in which they carried out their task.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
We read the speech from the throne very closely and several members, especially on the government side, seem very pleased with it.
The people are wondering if we are not slowly moving toward socialism with all the measures proposed in the speech from the throne.
As stated in that speech, the provinces will be called upon to approve an address to the Queen to allow for the amending of the constitution in Canada. That constitution was written a hundred years ago by people who were not Canadians, adopted by others who were not Canadians, kept by others who are not Canadians; as a nation, we have reached maturity and are able to shoulder our responsibilities. Why not leave that constitution where it is and write a new one taking into account the needs and aspirations of Canadians and remembering the two nations that built Canada.
I need not list all the points which, in our opinion, should be included in the constitution, because in my speech on the supplementary estimates during the last session, I dealt with those four points. Besides, our leader set them forth very effectively in his speech.
We learn in the speech from the throne that the government intends to set up a federal public welfare program. At the end of last session, the house passed Bill No. C-142 enabling the provinces to opt out from joint programs.
This legislation has been enacted only a few days ago, and the government has already decided to intrude in the provincial field and, what is more, this time under the pretext of helping the poor. Once again, the federal government is undermining provincial autonomy. Every attempt is being made to violate the constitution.
On many occasions we took a firm stand against the federal government when it inter-
April 13, 1365

The Address-Mr. Beaule fered in provincial fields and we intend to keep on doing just that this session.
If we want a strong Canada, a united Canada, a prosperous Canada, if we want to create a climate of unity in Canada, the federal government must stop infringing upon provincial jurisdictions; only then will we be able to say that a giant step has been taken toward unity.
Another item which caught my attention and that of all hon. members, is the one advocating war on poverty.
It is very difficult to understand how the Prime Minister will be able to declare war on poverty when the Premier of Quebec decides to fight to add new burdens to family budgets, particularly those of the Quebec workers.
How do you want to fight poverty with a premier, as in the province of Quebec, who levies taxes at will? Who is going to be affected the most by that new taxation other than the labour class?
In Ottawa, they have finally realized that there are, in Canada, some poor and destitute people. The government has just realized that action was necessary to fight hardship in Canada. While here in Ottawa they are getting ready to introduce legislation to cope with that ticklish problem-and we are anxious to know what kind of legislation the house will be called upon to discuss and vote-the Quebec premier, has not yet realized that there is hardship in Canada and also in his province.
In his ivory tower and in his jet plane, his head in the clouds, he drops a bomb filled with taxes on the province of Quebec.
If that is what we mean by fighting poverty and hardship; if that is what we mean by helping the little people and commiserating with the poor, then I am wondering if we are not laughing hypocritically at the people.
If the government really wishes to fight unemployment and poverty, it must enact spectacular measures, proclaim a broad public works program, reduce income tax, increase family allowances in keeping with the rise in the cost of living, increase veterans' allowances, raise the basic exemptions of individuals and grant a pre-salary to students.
Mr. Speaker, such spectacular measures would give a great impetus to the Canadian economy and increase our purchasing power.
Why wait until another war breaks out? We are asking the government to do in

peacetime what it can do in wartime to the advantage of the Canadian people.
The first report of the economic council of Canada was published a few weeks ago. It is an important survey of the Canadian economy and I do hope that it will not rot on the dusty shelves but that the government, the labouring classes and the business men will go through it and take appropriate measures.
In this report, the council is endeavouring to determine objectives and practical purposes for Canadians so as to secure, as much as possible, full employment, a fast rate of economic growth, price stabilization, to bring the balance of payments back to normal and to provide for a fair distribution of revenues. The thing to do is not to concentrate on one of those objectives, but to make all the necessary efforts in order to reach them all.
It is essential, I think, to secure a balanced development of the economy.
We have here in Canada specific problems that are not to be found elsewhere. For instance, in the field of labour we record a larger increase than any other industrialized country.
If the government wants to prevent the rise of unemployment above 3 per cent, it should endeavour to create 1,500,000 new jobs by 1970. To reach that goal, the Canadian economy will have to expand quickly and tremendously.
Another point contained in the brief, which is not the least, is the tax problem. If we reach our objectives, obviously, government expenditures will increase.
But the Canadian economy should expand more rapidly than government expenditures and, in this way, bring about a rapid and considerable increase in income, which would give the government the long awaited opportunity to alleviate the burden of taxes while spurring on the economy of the country.
This report from the council is not a planning report but one in which it is trying to place the facts in their true perspective.
I hope the government will duly consider this report.
I will now deal briefly with our relations with foreign countries.
What action will the government take regarding economic and cultural pressure exercised by the United States which we have heard so much about? It is high time we thought about it and prepare a plan of action. Is it necessary or desirable, in present circumstances, to divorce completely and drastically our economy from that of the
April 13. 1965

United States? Is it possible? Have we the necessary determination, courage and understanding to take decisions in this matter and abide by them?
What about our relations with China, Russia and other communist countries becoming important outlets for our wheat and other farm products, countries also interested in our industrial production? Can we carry on business with Red China while refusing to recognize its political existence?
What about our responsibilities toward the United Nations, NATO, GATT and other international bodies to which Canada belongs?
Considering the rapid economic, political and military evolution of the world today, Canada should be able to act quickly and firmly to protect its own interests and fulfil its commitments on the international scene. Are we so much preoccupied by our domestic problems, our regional and local issues, that our capacity to take some decisive action at the international level is hampered? Of course, those are questions which cannot be answered forthwith. However, they underline the complex problems and the difficult alternatives which are facing the country today.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
On the other hand, we are in a better position than ever before to create an economic and cultural climate favourable to all Canadians and to contribute to a considerable extent to peace and welfare in the world. Let us not forget that our problems must be faced and solved by a mature and united Canada having faith in its destiny.
Mr. Speaker, there is now another problem of tremendous concern to several members, organizations and Canadians: it is the peaceful revolution taking place in Quebec, and the Ralliement Creditiste has something to do with this ferment.
Whatever the Anglo-Saxons in our province might say, we are not extremists. And our so-called extremism is not, any more than history, the reason for our disagreement.
I am not aware in my time of a stranger and more appalling phenomenon than this desire to depreciate us morally and to accuse us of all the sins under the sun especially those we are not responsible for.
Our people have certainly been hurt and harassed in the last 150 years. We have often been deceived, humiliated and oppressed. But we can proudly assert that we have remained free from hate.
We have never given back blow for blow. We do not entertain the slightest desire for
The Address-Mr. Beaule revenge, we only want our little share of justice.
Nothing will be changed as long as no decision has been made to go to the root of the problem.
The first charity English and French Canadians owe each other, the prerequisite to good understanding is frankness.
The two races do not agree because one wants equal rights provided that it gets the lion's share. Deep down some English Canadians do not want to recognize and accept the French fact.
It is no longer necessary to wonder how the right to think, to feel, to act as French Canadians becomes in some people's opinion narrow provincialism.
Each time one of our rights was challenged, some of our political leaders asked us, for the sake of peace and national unity, to give up part of our heritage. And, for the sake of peace and national unity we yielded every time.
There was always members of Parliament, senators, ministers charged with rallying their compatriots, to take away from us, shred by shred, our heritage and our dignity.
Political history since confederation tells us that most of our so-called great men were primarily yes-men.
What remains to be done? We do not have to prove that we want national unity in Canada more than anybody else, since we have made more sacrifices for it than anybody else. We always keep our hand open and outstretched, but we no longer outstretch a limp hand to be crushed.
We do not refuse to co-operate, but cooperation must be mutual. Our co-operation is no longer inspired and directed by the slavishness of parties, but by the interests of the province and of our nation when those interests do not conflict with the general interests.
Let us be strong and conscious of our geographical position. In 1867, confederation would not have been possible without us, and we are still indispensable to the maintenance of confederation. We are the bridge linking east and west.
On the St. Lawrence we have the most beautiful harbours, and railway lines must go through our territory. The province of Quebec affords air lines their easiest landing fields.
Our lands are the best in Canada and in America. Let us no longer offer this wealth to foreigners for a mess of pottage.
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Beaule Let others day in and day out inveigh against provincialism.
To sum up, we will be respected the day we have our economy well in hand.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote an excerpt from an article by Andre Langvin which was published in the April 1965 issue of Le Magazine Maclean concerning the fame of our national institution:
It is obvious that all those turpitudes have fostered some sort of fatalism which, like a cancer, eats away at what we are bound to call our national conscience. That is the worst that could happen to us because to believe that, as an ethnical group, we can only engender dubious politicians or that the latter are such only because they come from our group is to believe that immorality in public affairs is connected with a biological phe-nomen.
Then, any attempt at cleaning up becomes an illusion and, worse still, seems to be the typical gimmick of the system. When our young men and women say openly: "All politicians are alike, they are only interested in making money", it is not so much the cruelty of their statement that is shocking as the kind of cynical submissiveness behind such a statement; it is a terrible admission of helplessness.
Therefore, on the one hand, those young men and women must be convinced that they will not necessarily inherit a sort of original sin, because there is no collective guilt and, on the other, that they will be encouraged to fight a rotten system instead of accepting with resignation the fact that it will only produce dishonest politicians. The system did not only permit this avalanche of scandals where so many of our fellow citizens were involved, it also encouraged their proliferation: a system which gives hidden powers to those who fill the electoral coffers, which forces the representative of the people to act as go-between in order to obtain preferential treatment, for his supporters, which stuffs the Senate and the legislative body with directors of large companies, which leads dozens of lawyers into conflicts of interests, confusing their duties as members of Parliament and their duties as professional men, permitting so many officials trained in government service to take advantage of their contacts and of their knowledge to secure employment with private firms, and which, finally, makes so many appointments and requests for services to the state dependant upon political allegiance.
All this of course can be remedied and legislation can be passed regarding all those matters in order to establish standards giving less leeway to elastic consciences. Every political party should be made to show the amount of its funds and the nature of contributions. Nobody will really believe in a complete reform of the provincial Liberal party as long as the Premier is against transferring the full and open control of the fund to members of the federation. The administration can be brought closer together, geographically as well as humanly, and a control agency could be created to which any citizen could appeal who considers himself wronged. Senators, legislative councillors and members of parliament could be forced to declare publicly their sources of income; the nation is too generous with them that they

might consider evading a mild obligation such as this. High officials might be prohibited for some time to enter the service of a business dealing with the department where they were employed. Finally, a non-political organization might be created to scrutinize the appointments made by the government and the list of persons called upon to render service.
It might be argued that this would hinder greatly the politicians and civil servants, and that this would be demanding more from them than from ordinary citizens. But whoever chooses to serve in the public service chooses also to be responsible for his actions, and the nation expects him to obey this code of ethics. The fact that this code is written in part can only reassure him. It is only at this price that the function of the politician will be revalorized, that we will escape this false collective guilt some are trying to pin on us, and that our young people made cynical by various happenings will be convinced that democracy does not necessarily mean corruption.

Mr. Speaker, in the interests of brevity may I quickly pass over the traditional compliments on the excellence of the members' speeches, with the suggestion that we remember what has been said over the last seven days, and in the days to come try to live up to the ambitions which have been expressed. If this is the case, I am sure that the sentiments expressed earlier this afternoon by the hon. Member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather), that the opinions of this House have possibly been overlooked by Provincial-Federal conferences in the West Block, will not be overlooked in the future. If we can contain ourselves and express ideas, instead of just making noise, then we will make a contribution to the Government of his country.
The Speech from the Throne dealt with many problems of the day and proposals for higher standards of living, proposals which will affect the lives of Canadians in all walks of life and in all areas of this wonderful country. I intend to touch on just a few of them which I feel are most important to my constituents and to Canadians of the nation.
First, I would like to draw hon. Members' attention to a lecture which was given by Mr. Peter F. Drucker, of the School of Business at the University of Toronto, last March. Professor Drucker's remarks have been widely publicized in the Canadian press and have created great interest not only among industry but also the professions. His remarks dealt with entrepreneurship in business. He stressed that certain companies do well year after year, that they consistently
April 13, 1965

outperform their competitors in good times or bad. One of the chief reasons for this was entrepreneurship.
Entrepreneurship has a specific subject matter, a specific concern. It is effectiveness. Entrepreneurship is not concerned with efficiency; that is the concern of management, or we might say, in the case of Government, the civil service. It is the subject of managerial discipline. Efficiency attempts to do things the right way. It deals with quality, rather than the quantity of results and output.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Efficiency of course is not unimportant, but no business or government can continue to survive or give the leadership required of it because it is efficient. Unless it does the right things, unless it has a degree of effectiveness, it cannot live at all, no matter how efficient it may be. It is also true that a Government that does the right thing can tolerate inefficiency, it can tolerate abuse, and it can tolerate these things without suffering too much. Entrepreneurship, then, is knowing what things to do; it is not how to do them. Mr. Speaker, if the continued success of the Liberal Party over the last 30 years is to be attributed to a special ability, then surely that ability must be the art of doing the right thing.
Many Canadians have said that the Liberals were just plain lucky to be defeated in 1957. I believe there are a few Ministers on the front bench that can be excluded from that group. Many Canadians said that the forces of recession were building up and could not be stopped. They said it was a product of Liberal administration. Whatever the cause, whatever the case, it was a situation that had to be met. It was a time for entrepreneurial decisions; because unemployment was becoming a national problem at that time and it was top editorial material, instead of flags or furniture or fighting, interparty style. I remember a statement that was made by the Labour Minister at that time. I am thinking of the winter of 1961-62. As I remember, he said that the Government had done all it could; now it was up to industry to correct mass unemployment. Well, Sir, that lacks entrepreneurship; it lacks imagination; it lacks the art of being able to do the right thing. That was just one example, and there are many that I am not going to quote this evening because of the time. But, contrast, if you will, the simple move, the oh so effective move, the $500
The Address-Mr. Morison winter building bonus. In one stroke winter unemployment in this country was well on the way to being licked.
There are other examples; the Columbia River Treaty, the Seaway project, the Crown Corporations and the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, the latter both being set up by Mr. C. D. Howe, with his exceptional flair for being able to do the right thing- possibly politics might be excluded from that. Each and every example I have given is one of doing what was required at the right time.

The Unemployment Insurance Fund was an example of doing what had to be done. Unfortunately, through Government inefficiency, which I mentioned earlier-I am thinking of the previous Government, of course-its effectiveness has been hampered.
Let us look, Mr. Speaker, to entrepeneur-ship in the future; the proposals in the Throne Speech. First I would like to mention the lessening of international tension. I do not know what confidential advice was given to the President of the United States by our Prime Minister. In fact, I do not know if L.B.J. really knew he was getting advice-

-but I do believe that with the deft ability of our Prime Minister-and this is his forte-the message of doing the right thing got across to Mr. Johnson and I do believe that a contribution has already been made in the touchy area of international peace. Second, is the matter of the Conference of Commonwealth Prime Ministers to discuss the expansion of trade and the establishment of a Commonwealth Secretariat. We in this Government, Mr. Speaker, are vitally aware of the changes that must come in our trading pattern with Great Britain. For years past this great and bountiful mother country has favoured us at every turn with trading privileges; always giving, always asking very little in return. Today this generosity is no longer possible. England is struggling for her economic life, combating trade deficits, financial problems and inefficient production. We in Canada, taking only 12 per cent of her exports, contribute to almost 23.5 per cent of her trade imbalance. England can no longer afford to tolerate this situation and she must seek from us a new trading pattern.
April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Morison
I support our automobile agreement. In this vital segment of our industry there is the greatest opportunity for the increased employment of Canadians. But as we ratify this agreement, let us produce an equally brilliant plan so that the United Kingdom industries will not suffer; and if this is not possible, let us not be shackled by old ideas, by trading defeats in the past. There are new markets. Is industrial trade with the Soviet Union out of the question? They buy our wheat; why not our machinery and technology? Britain, France and other western countries have the major part of a new billion-dollar market that has emerged from Russia in the last few years. As I say, this is a new market. Why cannot Canada lead into new market areas and ideas, where success is to be found ahead of those who wait in hopes of an easier path?
Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but recall the many letters I received during the flag debate concerning traditional ties, allegiance to the mother country, the breaking of honourable connections. They were just words, Mr. Speaker. Our Government's proposal to form a secretariat to bring England and the Commonwealth closer together and work to their mutual advantage is more than that. It is constructive work. It is the ability to do the right thing, to seek accomplishment through deeds and not words.
We must be entrepreneurs if we are going to find the wealth necessary to finance our war on poverty, which brings me to my third observation. At the outset let me say that I am aware that in an affluent society, as we have in Canada today-the third wealthiest nation in the world; a nation which has an average income per capita of $1,800; a nation that is on the threshold of an ever more expanding and technically sophisticated economy-there is going to be a widening gap between the honest hard worker and those who are not-

speechtext:
-or those who, for one reason or another, just cannot compete in the labour market.
Mr. Speaker, those remarks on the other side of the House almost make me wonder whether I should not be addressing my remarks to them.
Into this gap the three levels of Government, Federal, Provincial and Municipal, poured almost 4 billion last year, almost twice as much as ten years ago. I do not believe there are twice as many poor in this country or that they need twice as much

welfare; but I do believe that a complete overhaul of our welfare programs is necessary.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Today welfare is a part of our society. It must provide the basic needs for its people or they will turn to socialism. We have had welfare programs of a spotty character for years. They have been expensive but they have not always been adequate. We needed family allowances in this country. We needed assistance to education if our labour force was going to meet the modern challenge. We must help the disabled, the blind and the old, or we will have a social revolution on our hands. But we must do this for another reason too, and business must understand this as well.
We must try to raise the standards of our people. If Government does not do this, business will suffer. Business, if consistently asked for charitable contributions to community chests, to universities and to all kinds of charitable enterprise to assist the needy, the helpless, the sick, will really wonder whether or not it is helping worthy causes. The Speech from the Throne recognizes this problem. The Government plans to review with the Provinces the whole picture of the welfare field. This plan is not to instal Socialism; it is to avoid Socialism.
I have not dealt with specific areas like the Labour Code, the Pension Plan or medicare. Perhaps I should, because nobody thinks that the Labour Code is perfect. The minimum wage is certainly not out of line and the hours of work provisions, generally speaking, are found in collective agreements, although there are some industries where they do not apply. The Minister has authority to provide the necessary exemptions in these cases, and I think he will do so.
The Pension Plan is needed, in my view, and too many people have no opportunity to help provide for their old age. The Pension Plan now provides for a minimum, and an employee in order to achieve this minimum will contribute less than $80 a year.
Medicare is a very involved subject. The Federal authorities cannot undertake it alone. This program must be developed cautiously, through experience and by working with the Provinces. It cannot be developed in a way which will slow down the economy, and in this regard we must be prudent.
My fourth observation deals with the agricultural segment of the population. It was
April 13, 1965
revealing to me when campaigning in rural "Wentworth to hear on many occasions that old question: Why vote Liberal, they never do anything for the farmer. Not being a farmer or a student of agricultural history, I found this a rather difficult point to debate, especially when I knew the western boys were getting fat. Wheat payments were being made, and although the local press did not give that fact much publicity, the word did get around. On my next trip to the farms of Wentworth I will be able to refer to the many good things that have been done for farmers. Who is a bigger entrepreneur than Harry Hays? He knows what the farmers *vant and is impatient to have the Govern-nent carry out his programs. These programs vill not be give-aways, but based on sound jractical policies to assist the Eastern farmer ,o become a part of an efficient and profitable farming community.
Originally the word "entrepreneur" referred to a single individual, and we might still think of such a man as an isolated individual. On the other hand, as soon as an individual has attained the slightest amount of success, he builds an organization for continuing success.
Mr. Speaker, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that the latter half of the 20th century belongs to Canada. May the Liberal Party continue to be the entrepreneur to fulfil this prophecy.

I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I will be brief because I do not believe that traditionally a supporter of the Government should conclude this debate. Perhaps that is not a good reason for speaking, but let me say that I do have a few remarks I wish to make.
At several points the previous speaker bragged about the Liberal record, particularly with reference to the $1,800 per capita income. I wish the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) had been present in the House when the hon. Member made that statement, because it is precisely in this regard that the Minister of Agriculture has failed as an entrepreneur. That Minister may know 22620-25
The Address-Mr. Winkler what the farmers want in some respects, but he has not manifested good sense as far as the incomes of Eastern farmers are concerned.
I asked the Minister a question this morning regarding the price of cheese. His reply indicated at least to me that the producers of cheese milk will receive less this year than they did last year. It is my humble opinion that the Government is making a determined effort to avoid supporting this particular segment of the dairy industry. One can only wait to see what will happen in this regard, but I hope my words will have some bearing on the Government's attitude toward the producers of this product in Eastern Canada.
The Speech from the Throne was an exercise in the creation of hypocrisies. The Government has brought forward a great number of promised programs, but it remains to be seen whether they will carry them forward in the form of legislation. The secret right now, as to whether this will happen, lies in the knowledge of what will be contained in the budget which is to brought down the Monday following the Easter recess. I am sure that if it contains as many hypocrisies as are contained in the Throne Speech an election is imminent. I am not afraid of an election, but realize that it is an old Liberal trick to fill the Speech from the Throne and the Budget with all kinds of promises in the hope that the electorate will believe in them. It is well known on this side of the House that some of the Ministers went out of their way a couple of nights ago to keep Members out of the House, with the hope that the Government would be defeated, and they would be forced to call an election.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It was obvious that these Ministers wanted to go to the country, but could not convince the old guard that this was now a propitious time or that this was a good tactic. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), who is an enthusiastic individual, holds the key to this situation. He holds that key and we will wait to see what comes out in the Budget.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
As I look over the items in the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, I note, as other Members have noted, the reference to the Government's war on poverty. This is a great big joke to me, when I think of the whole mass of Government members standing up and voting against $100 old age security for people 65 years of age and over, when they knew full well they could have done

April 13, 1965

The Address-Mr. Winkler so without charging the taxpayers one cent. This was possible. It was spelled out. Even my friends on the left voted against it, and that does not matter to me, but the fact is that now the Government talks about a war on poverty.
I said once before in the course of this session that if they want to come along with me and look at some of the cases I deal with on week ends they will see how people have to live on $75 a month in this Liberal Government high cost of living era. I hope the Member for Hamilton, whatever his riding is, or Wentworth, will take that home with him because he will have exactly the same experiences. If he had to live on $75 a month he might have decided to stand up and vote for the responsible amendment put forward by our party at that time.
Another thing that is very topical this evening is something that the Government missed. They have covered everything else. I think the Member for Wentworth said that the Government has recognized every problem, and certainly the Speech from the Throne would appear to cover every problem; but they have missed one. What the Government should have said in the Speech from the Throne is: My Ministers believe it is high time that the Press Gallery be removed from the Centre Block. Tonight the members of the Press Gallery have got their answer. They have got to get out. This would have been the fastest action that this Government ever took. I understand that the members of the Press Gallery were advised today that their time in the Centre Block is finished. I believe this is going to ruin a certain fundamental tradition around here which everybody more or less appreciates. I think arrangements might have been made to retain that particular facility in this building. However, the Government is acting in its usual dictatorial manner and it is going to fix everything and kick them out of the Centre Block. That is the fate of the Press Gallery this evening.
I promised to be brief, Mr. Speaker, but I want to make a few remarks about my constituency. The Speech from the Throne has indicated the desire of the Government to expand the development program for low income areas. No one likes to brag about coming from a low income area, but I have a letter here similar to that referred to by the hon. Member for Port Arthur. It comes from the Georgian Bay Development Association which encompasses a number of counties running all the way from Bruce right up to the top. I

would imagine it goes right up to the Prime Minister's constituency.
The letter is signed by the president of the Association, a very well known Liberal in the area. He pleads with the Government to take action. He even thanks them for what they have set forth in their Throne Speech, and I wifi too if they carry it out; but this has not been the case in the past. There are a number of counties in that area, Mr. Speaker, that are eligible in every sense of the word to be named designated areas, but where do these designations occur? If the Government were acting responsibly they would take this entire area from Lake Huron right around to the north end of Georgian Bay and make it a designated area, so that at least the people would have the opportunity to offer something to industries that might come there.
Even the agricultural people of these counties, who are well known in almost every field of mixed farming endeavour, are experiencing a continuing decline in their income, and I have also mentioned that before in the House. They rarely reach the level of $1,800 mentioned by the hon. Member for Wentworth. He should come with me and see what these people have to say. Since this Government took office the incomes of agricultural producers in this area have gone down and down and down. We have these great promises in the Speech from the Throne and I hope the Government lives up to them. I will be one of those who will vote for them, if they can show me a program that is going to increase the income of farmers.
We have a few very basic indigenous industries there that we want to retain, because they are very prosperous. The Government knows why they are prospeous. I have mentioned this to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp). He knows the problem very well and I hope he does not place them in an embarrassing position such as we fear by reason of what might happen through further movement toward free trade.
As a matter of fact, I have a clipping of a speech made by the Minister in Kitchener during the Christmas recess, which indicates he is beginning to have second thoughts about free trade, and I hope he will keep the industries of my constituency closely in mind. We will support him as long as he does not sell us out.
At the time that the Government changed there were two major projects under way in our area that could have helped the whole area financially and economically. One was

the establishment of a national park in Bruce County, and in my humble opinion this still remains a very important factor in regard to the economy of that area, which is now one of the black areas on the map of Ontario. In other words, it is a poverty area. I promoted this park. I do not know what is being done about it today. I almost had it to the point of being consummated at the time the Government changed. I have discussed it with the relevant Minister and I hope he will read these words and do something about the matter, because now it is not just something we would like to have but rather almost a necessity.
I must also make reference to the visit of a few weeks ago of the Prime Minister and his entourage to the County of Northumberland.
I have forgotten the name of the town, but he turned the sod there for a new penitentiary. It happens to be one that the Liberals stole for patronage purposes from the constituency of Grey-Bruce and placed in the County of the hon. Lady. The hon. Lady has a little more influence than I thought she had, but I can tell you that the people of Grey-Bruce will not forget it, because the Liberal Association of that riding supported every move to have that penitentiary located there, for economic reasons. It was the subject of the first letter I wrote after going into opposition and I informed the highest authorities m the Government accordingly. I would also say in conclusion-

The Address-Mr. Herridge Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West): Mr. Speaker, I rise seething with indignation to bring a question of privilege to the attention of the House. I have in my hand a statement issued by Davidson Dunton and Andre Laurendeau, co-chairmen of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, under date of April 13, 1965. You will remember the excellent attitude taken by the Prime Minister toward a certain questionnaire. I will simply read the concluding two paragraphs. A great deal of the statement is explanatory but this is what it has to say in part:
We believe, therefore, that the survey should continue on the same voluntary confidential basis as before. If refusals become too high the interviews, of course, will be stopped. Sixty seven Members have already been interviewed and only eight others have refused to date. As long as a high response rate continues, the interviews will go on unchanged.
The Commission has been charged with carrying out an inquiry; and that in fact is precisely what it is trying to do.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Surely in all good sense it should not be hampered or blocked as it endeavours to fulfil the purpose for which it was established; nor be called on continually to justify the methods which after careful consideration it deems suitable. We believe this would be a dangerous precedent from which the work of this and other royal commissions could suffer.
My point of privilege is that I think this is a gross piece of impertinence with regard to the Prime Minister of our country and his efforts to protect the rights of Members of Parliament of all parties, and his efforts to protect their privileges and their privacy.
